### Sparse updates {#sec-edge-intelligence-sparse-updates-879b}

Sparse updates adapt selected existing parameters rather than adding modules. Their expressivity relative to adapters depends on the selected locations and parameter budget. A task-adaptive policy selects those locations using evidence about the current task or user. The resulting update space can target changes that a fixed subset misses, but selection itself consumes resources and does not guarantee that the complete training path fits the device.

The useful savings depend on what the runtime can omit. Unselected parameters need no gradient or optimizer state, but their operations may still lie on the backward path to selected parameters. A policy must therefore compare the measured update cost with its adaptation benefit; the fraction of trainable parameters alone does not predict the reduction in compute.

The key insight is that layers do not contribute equally to local performance gains. If the system can identify the minimal subset with the highest adaptation value, it can spend scarce training capacity where it changes the model's behavior most.

#### Sparse update design {#sec-edge-intelligence-sparse-update-design-ee7c}

Let a neural network be defined by parameters $\theta = \{\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_{\NumberOfLayers}\}$ across $\NumberOfLayers$ layers. In standard fine-tuning, gradients are computed and updates are performed on all parameters:
$$
\theta_i \leftarrow \theta_i - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_i}, \quad \text{for } i = 1, \ldots, \NumberOfLayers
$$

In task-adaptive sparse updates, the system selects a small subset $\mathcal{S} \subset \{1, \ldots, \NumberOfLayers\}$ such that only parameters in $\mathcal{S}$ are updated:
$$
\theta_i \leftarrow
\begin{cases}
\theta_i - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_i}, & \text{if } i \in \mathcal{S} \\
\theta_i, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The challenge lies in selecting the optimal subset $\mathcal{S}$ given memory and compute constraints. A principled strategy is contribution analysis\index{Contribution Analysis!layer selection}, an empirical method that estimates how much each layer contributes to downstream performance improvement. For example, one can measure the marginal gain from updating each layer independently:

1. Freeze the entire model.
2. Unfreeze one candidate layer.
3. Finetune briefly and evaluate improvement in validation accuracy.
4. Rank layers by performance gain per unit cost (e.g., per KB of trainable memory).

This layer-wise profiling yields a candidate ranking from which $\mathcal{S}$ can be constructed subject to a memory budget. Gains measured one layer at a time need not add when layers train together, and shared backward dependencies change the combined cost. The selected set therefore needs a joint quality and resource check, with the profiling cost included in the adaptation budget.

@Fig-ondevice-pretraining places that ranking inside a complete selective fine-tuning\index{Fine-Tuning!selective, on-device} pipeline. Stage 1 meta-trains the network in the cloud, which means training its initial weights so that a few later updates on new data adapt it well (the idea behind model-agnostic meta-learning, taken up in @sec-edge-intelligence-federated-personalization-3c73). Stage 2 ranks layers or channel groups by adaptation benefit per unit of device cost and lets the device budget set the cut, and Stage 3 updates only the units above the cut on local data. Freezing the units below the cut removes their gradient and optimizer state, but the backward pass still runs through any frozen layer that lies between the loss and a selected one, so the selected set must be costed under the complete execution schedule.

::: {#fig-ondevice-pretraining fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Selective on-device fine-tuning**: (1) The full network is meta-trained in the cloud on generic data. (2) Each layer or channel group is ranked by its expected adaptation benefit per unit of device cost, and the device's data, compute, and memory budget sets the cut. (3) On the device, only units above the cut are updated on local data while the rest stay frozen. Scores and cut position are schematic." fig-alt="Three stages. Stage 1, meta-train in the cloud: layers 1 to 3 and a head, all blue and trainable. An arrow labeled theta leads to stage 2, rank: horizontal bars for each layer, short gray bars for layers 1 and 2 and long blue bars for layer 3 and the head, with a red dashed cut line rising from a dashed box labeled device budget, data, compute, memory. An arrow labeled mask leads to stage 3, update on device: layers 1 and 2 gray and frozen, layer 3 and head blue and trainable."}
![](images/svg/ondevice-pretraining.svg)

:::

A concrete example is TinyTrain, a method designed to allow rapid adaptation on-device [@kwon2024tinytrain]. TinyTrain combines offline preparation with a task-adaptive sparse-update method that dynamically selects layers or channels to update using user data, memory limits, and compute limits. At runtime, the system updates only the selected subset rather than treating the whole network as trainable.

In implementation, selective layer updating\index{Selective layer updating!execution} turns the ranking into `requires_grad` decisions or equivalent graph masks. @Lst-selective-update extends this pattern to profiling-driven layer selection, demonstrating how hardware profiling determines which layers to update based on contribution scores and memory constraints.

::: {#lst-selective-update lst-cap="**Selective Layer Updating**: This technique allows fine-tuning specific layers of a pretrained model while keeping others frozen, optimizing computational resources for targeted improvements."}

```{.python}
# Selective layer update based on contribution analysis
# Layers selected via profiling: conv2 and fc have highest
# accuracy-per-KB impact for this task

for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    if "conv2" in name or "fc" in name:
        param.requires_grad = True  # Train high-impact layers
    else:
        param.requires_grad = False  # Freeze low-impact layers

# Parameter fraction follows layer shapes; adaptation quality requires evaluation
# Memory savings: gradient storage only for selected layers
```

:::

TinyTrain makes the runtime motivation concrete. Consider a scenario where a user wears an augmented reality headset that performs real-time object recognition. As lighting and environments shift, the system must adapt to maintain accuracy, but training must occur during brief idle periods or while charging. TinyTrain addresses this constraint through task-adaptive sparse updates: the deployment process selects a small update set that fits the device's memory and compute budget. The approach keeps adaptation fast, energy-efficient, and memory-aware when the target task and device profile match the method's assumptions.

Task-adaptive sparse updates still introduce system-level trade-offs. Contribution analysis has a nontrivial computational cost even when it occurs during pretraining or initial profiling, so the deployment pipeline must budget for it. Stability also requires attention: if too few parameters are selected for updating, the model may underfit the target distribution, so teams need validation thresholds for the selected subset before deployment. The selection policy must also account for hardware-specific execution costs because some parameters show high contribution scores but prove expensive to update on certain architectures. Despite these trade-offs, task-adaptive sparse updates provide a practical mechanism to scale adaptation across deployment contexts from microcontrollers to mobile devices [@kwon2024tinytrain].

#### Adaptation strategy comparison {#sec-edge-intelligence-adaptation-strategy-comparison-1faf}

The design target is the smallest update space that captures the local change. Full fine-tuning pays every term of @eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory; bias-only updates and head-only training fit minor calibration or new output categories; LoRA and residual adapters add bounded capacity beside a frozen backbone; task-adaptive sparse updates spend profiling effort to select valuable existing parameters. A larger update space is justified only if the measured quality gain fits the device's training budget. @Tbl-adaptation-strategies collects these adaptation strategy trade-offs\index{Adaptation strategy!trade-offs}, keyed to the budget term each one shrinks, so the choice can be checked against expressivity, runtime support, and selection cost.

| **Technique**            |       **Trainable Parameters**      |               **Memory Overhead**              |   **Expressivity**   | **Use Case Suitability**                    | **System Requirements**                         |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------:|:--------------------:|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------|
| **Full Fine-Tuning**     |            All parameters           |    Highest; every term of the peak budget      |        Highest       | Large domain shift on capable devices       | Full backward support and memory headroom       |
| **Bias-Only Updates**    |           Bias terms only           |  Minimal $M_{\text{train}}$; activations remain |          Low         | Simple personalization; low variance        | Extreme memory/compute limits                   |
| **Head-Only Training**   |           Final classifier          | Minimal; backward pass stops at the head       |          Low         | New output classes; custom wake words       | Frozen encoder; reusable cached features        |
| **LoRA**                 | Low-rank factors per adapted matrix |    Low $M_{\text{train}}$; activations remain   |   Moderate to High   | One mergeable adaptation per user           | Merge step and requantization check for serving |
| **Residual Adapters**    |           Adapter modules           |    Low $M_{\text{train}}$; activations remain   |   Moderate to High   | Switching among several contexts on mobile  | Mobile-class SoCs with runtime support          |
| **Sparse Layer Updates** |     Selective parameter subsets     |  Variable; depends on the selected layers      | High (task-adaptive) | Real-time adaptation; domain shift          | Requires profiling or meta-training             |

: **Adaptation Strategy Trade-Offs**: Six approaches to model adaptation compared by trainable parameters, the term of the peak-memory budget (@eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory) they shrink, expressivity, suitability, and system requirements. Methods that shrink only the trainable state $M_{\text{train}}$ still keep the activations their backward pass needs, while head-only training also removes most of the activation term by stopping the backward pass at the classifier. {#tbl-adaptation-strategies}

Once an adaptation mechanism fits the device's memory and execution budget, it must still learn from the available examples. Reducing trainable state does not create labels or ensure that a user's recent observations represent future use. The next constraint is therefore statistical: extracting reliable learning signal from sparse local data while retaining useful prior behavior.

## Data Efficiency {#sec-edge-intelligence-data-efficiency-c701}

A user corrects smartphone keyboard autocorrect perhaps three times a day. The system cannot require 10,000 labeled sentences to train a local language model. Data efficiency at the edge means learning aggressively from a sparse, noisy, and uncurated trickle of implicit user feedback, maximizing the signal extracted from each interaction.

The systems trade-off is data collection cost against adaptation quality. Every retained example costs user friction, energy, storage, and privacy exposure. A voice assistant adapting to speech samples weighs model improvement against battery drain and user comfort with always-on recording, and a keyboard chooses between logging shallow keystroke statistics and keeping full typing sessions. Unlike a central pipeline, the device cannot reach into a larger dataset when its own evidence runs short, and an application that needs a decision before enough evidence accumulates may be better served by a validated fixed model than by immediate learning. Whatever the device does learn must also stay compatible with the adaptation mechanism of @sec-edge-intelligence-model-adaptation-6a82 and with any federated protocol that later consumes it.

The strategy choice depends on which scarcity binds first, and practical systems usually combine several. Few-shot learning fits cases where a few labeled or weakly labeled examples must drive personalization. Streaming updates fit settings where useful data arrives incrementally and cannot be batched in advance. Experience replay spends memory to stabilize continual updates by reusing scarce examples. Data compression reduces the storage cost of those histories so replay and lightweight training remain feasible within edge memory budgets. Data scarcity thus becomes an allocation problem, in which the device spends labels, memory, compute, and privacy budget where they produce the most reliable local signal.

### Few-shot learning and data streaming {#sec-edge-intelligence-fewshot-learning-data-streaming-566e}

In conventional machine learning workflows, effective training typically requires large labeled datasets, carefully curated and preprocessed to ensure sufficient diversity and balance. On-device learning, by contrast, must often proceed from only a handful of local examples, collected passively through user interaction or ambient sensing, and rarely labeled in a supervised fashion. These constraints motivate two complementary adaptation strategies: few-shot learning, in which models generalize from a small, static set of examples, and streaming adaptation\index{Streaming adaptation!continuous updates}, where incremental observations support updates scheduled within device budgets.

Few-shot adaptation uses limited labeled or weakly labeled evidence for a new task or user condition [@wang2020]. Bias-only updates, adapter modules, and prototype-based classification restrict what must be learned, but each still needs validation against overfitting. Let $\mathcal{D}_{\text{shot}} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n_{\text{shot}}}$ denote the local support set; here $n_{\text{shot}}$ counts all examples in the set, rather than examples per class. A candidate policy might permit few gradient steps ($n_{\text{steps}} \ll 100$) and a small trainable subset ($|\theta_{\text{updated}}| \ll |\theta|$). These are illustrative restrictions, not universal feasibility conditions. The actual step and parameter budgets follow from measured device cost and the quality target, including retained performance on earlier tasks.

Keyword spotting (KWS) systems are a common target for data-efficient on-device adaptation; Speech Commands provides a dataset for training and evaluating limited-vocabulary KWS models [@warden2018speech]. A detector must distinguish its target phrase from background speech while meeting latency and false-activation requirements. One design uses a pretrained acoustic encoder, such as a small convolutional or recurrent network, to map audio into embeddings for a lightweight classifier. A shared encoder supplies reusable features, while local examples can support a custom wake word or an underrepresented accent. Whether those examples justify local training depends on their coverage, transfer restrictions, and the improvement over the shared detector.

Few-shot adaptation can train an output classifier or another small parameter subset from utterances collected directly on the device\index{Wake-word detection!few-shot adaptation}. A user might provide 5–10 recordings of a custom wake word while the acoustic encoder remains frozen. Those positive examples define what to recognize, but the false-activation rate on other speech and background noise is a separate measurement, and the personalized detector should not be accepted until it has been made.

Head-only adaptation is cheap in a way the peak-memory budget of @eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory makes precise. Because the backward pass stops at the classifier, the encoder's saved activations leave the activation term, and the encoder outputs for the support set can be computed once and reused across update steps. What remains is running the encoder forward, holding the support examples or their features, and evaluating the adapted classifier. Those costs, not the size of the head, decide whether the update fits a particular phone or microcontroller.

Beyond static few-shot learning, many on-device scenarios benefit from streaming adaptation, where models must learn incrementally as new data arrives [@hayes2020remind]. Streaming adaptation generalizes this idea to continuous, asynchronous settings where data arrives incrementally over time. Let $\{x_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$ represent the observations selected from the stream for admitted updates. In streaming settings, observations arrive continuously, but the runtime admits training only when memory, energy, and foreground-latency budgets permit. The following rule describes one admitted update; it does not require a gradient step on every arrival. The index $t$ counts these update steps. The computable loss may come from implicit feedback, pseudo-labels, self-supervised objectives, reconstruction error, or a task-specific proxy rather than explicit human labels. The model update can be written generically as:
$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta_t \nabla \mathcal{L}(x_t; \theta_t)
$$
where $\eta_t$ is the learning rate at time $t$. This form of adaptation is sensitive to noise and drift in the input distribution, and thus often incorporates mechanisms such as learning rate decay, meta-learned initialization, or update gating to improve stability.

Aside from KWS, practical examples of these strategies abound. In wearable health devices, a model that classifies physical activities may begin with a generic classifier and adapt to user-specific motion patterns using only a few labeled activity segments. In smart assistants, user voice profiles are fine-tuned over time using ongoing speech input, even when explicit supervision is unavailable. Local corrections, repetitions, or downstream task completion can provide implicit signals, but only after the system defines which event counts as feedback and tests its validity. A user may accept a suggestion because it is convenient rather than correct, abandon a task for reasons unrelated to the model, or correct an error that the model itself induced. Production adaptation should therefore separate observed events from inferred labels, retain a nonadapting control cohort, measure delayed outcomes when available, and gate learning when the proxy-to-outcome relationship drifts.

Few-shot and streaming adaptation form the foundation for more advanced memory and replay strategies that address the stability challenges of continuous on-device learning.

### Experience replay {#sec-edge-intelligence-experience-replay-737e}

:::: {#dfn-edge-intelligence-catastrophic-forgetting .callout-definition title="Catastrophic forgetting"}

***Catastrophic forgetting***\index{Catastrophic Forgetting!definition} is the phenomenon in which a neural network trained sequentially on new tasks or data distributions rapidly loses performance on previously learned tasks, because gradient updates that optimize the new objective overwrite weight configurations that supported the old ones.

1.  **Significance**: Without explicit mitigation, fine-tuning a deployed classifier on a new domain can sharply reduce prior-task accuracy, even when the new domain is closely related to the old one [@kirkpatrick2017]. This is the central failure mode of on-device and federated learning: every device that adapts locally to its user's recent data risks erasing the general capabilities the centralized training run paid for, and the loss is invisible until inference encounters out-of-recent-context inputs.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike overfitting (a generalization failure on a single fixed task) and distribution shift (a deployment-time mismatch between training and inference data), forgetting is a training-time phenomenon caused by the sequential structure of the update stream itself; updates for new data can interfere with earlier solutions even when a representation capable of supporting both tasks exists.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a small experience-replay buffer is sufficient protection. A small buffer can hold aggregate accuracy on a held-out set while rare classes, which it samples too seldom, continue to degrade. Forgetting must therefore be measured per class or per cohort, and the remedies range from capacity-proportional or prioritized buffers to weight-regularization methods such as elastic weight consolidation, which store no examples (@sec-edge-intelligence-lifelong-adaptation-without-forgetting-9200).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_edge_intelligence_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two trend lines: green new-task performance rises while red old-task accuracy falls."}

*Learning the new task erodes accuracy on the old one.*
:::

::::

Experience replay addresses forgetting by retaining examples from earlier learning episodes and reusing them during later updates. Replay also appears in reinforcement learning [@mnih2015]; here its role is to keep earlier local observations represented as new data arrives. It is one stability mechanism with an explicit storage cost. @Sec-edge-intelligence-lifelong-adaptation-without-forgetting-9200 returns to the problem with parameter-importance penalties, bounded update footprints, and rollback.

Unlike server-side replay strategies that rely on large datasets and extensive compute, on-device replay must operate with extremely limited capacity, often with tens or hundreds of samples, and must avoid interfering with user experience [@rolnick2019experience]. Buffers may store only compressed features or distilled summaries, and updates must occur opportunistically (e.g., during idle cycles or charging). These system-level constraints reshape how replay is implemented and evaluated in the context of embedded ML.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ represent a memory buffer that retains a fixed-size subset of training examples. At time step $t$, the model receives a new data point $(x_t, y_t)$ and appends it to $\mathcal{M}$. A replay-based update then samples a batch $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{\BatchSize}$ of size $\BatchSize$ from $\mathcal{M}$ and applies a gradient step:
$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \left[ \frac{1}{\BatchSize} \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \mathcal{L}(x_i, y_i; \theta_t) \right]
$$
This is the streaming update of @sec-edge-intelligence-fewshot-learning-data-streaming-566e with one change of data source, from the newest observation to a batch drawn from $\mathcal{M}$. The systems cost lies in what that change requires, namely buffer storage that competes with model state and forward and backward work on old examples in every admitted window. Over time, this replay mechanism allows the model to reinforce prior knowledge while incorporating new information.

A practical on-device implementation might use a ring buffer to store a small set of compressed feature vectors rather than full input examples. @Lst-replay-buffer implements this minimal replay buffer\index{Replay buffer!circular ring design} design, demonstrating how a circular storage mechanism enables efficient memory management while balancing historical knowledge retention with new information incorporation.

::: {#lst-replay-buffer lst-cap="**Replay Buffer**: Implements a circular storage mechanism for efficient memory management in constrained environments. This approach allows models to efficiently retain and sample from recent data points, balancing the need to use historical information while incorporating new insights."}

```{.python}
import random


# Ring buffer for experience replay on memory-constrained devices
# Stores compressed features (not raw inputs) to minimize footprint
class ReplayBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity  # Fixed size, e.g., 1000 examples
        self.buffer = []
        self.index = 0  # Circular write pointer

    def store(self, feature_vec, label):
        if len(self.buffer) < self.capacity:
            self.buffer.append((feature_vec, label))  # Fill phase
        else:
            self.buffer[self.index] = (
                feature_vec,
                label,
            )  # Overwrite oldest
        self.index = (self.index + 1) % self.capacity  # Wrap around

    def sample(self, k):
        # Uniform sampling within the retained buffer; older examples are absent
        return random.sample(self.buffer, min(k, len(self.buffer)))
```

:::

This implementation maintains a fixed-capacity cyclic buffer, storing compressed representations (e.g., last-layer embeddings) and associated labels. Uniform sampling here covers only the retained recent window; it does not remove the history bias introduced by overwriting old examples. Reservoir sampling is an alternative when the goal is to represent the full stream, though any finite buffer still requires coverage checks.

In TinyML applications,\index{TinyML!experience replay} experience replay has been applied to problems such as gesture recognition, where devices must continuously improve predictions while observing a small number of events per day. Instead of training directly on the streaming data, the device stores representative feature vectors from recent gestures and uses them to finetune classification boundaries periodically. Similarly, in on-device keyword spotting, replaying past utterances can improve wake-word detection accuracy\index{Wake-word detection!experience replay} without the need to transmit audio data off-device.

Experience replay spends storage and additional update work to preserve earlier behavior. Raw inputs can exceed storage or retention budgets, especially in vision and audio applications. Cached feature vectors reduce that footprint, but an update starting from those vectors trains the downstream model without reconstructing the original encoder computation. If the encoder changes, old features may no longer match its current representation; the system must retain a compatible encoder, refresh the features from retained inputs, or expire incompatible entries. Persistent replay also consumes flash write cycles. Buffer contents, representation versions, and replay frequency therefore belong in the same resource and retention policy.

### Data compression {#sec-edge-intelligence-data-compression-8b40}

In many on-device learning scenarios, the raw training data may be too large, noisy, or redundant to store and process effectively. This motivates the use of compressed data representations, where the original inputs are transformed into lower-dimensional embeddings or compact encodings that preserve salient information while minimizing memory and compute costs.

Compressed representations serve two complementary goals: they reduce the footprint of stored data, allowing devices to maintain longer histories or replay buffers under tight memory budgets [@hayes2020remind], and they simplify the learning task by projecting raw inputs into more structured feature spaces, often learned via pretraining or meta-learning, in which efficient adaptation is possible with minimal supervision.

One common approach is to encode data points using a pretrained feature extractor and discard the original high-dimensional input. For example, an image $x_i$ might be passed through a CNN to produce an embedding vector $z_i = f(x_i)$, where $f(\cdot)$ is a fixed feature encoder. This embedding captures visual structure (e.g., shape, texture, or spatial layout) in a compact representation, usually ranging from 64 to 512 dimensions, suitable for lightweight downstream adaptation.

Mathematically, training can proceed over compressed samples $(z_i, y_i)$ using a lightweight decoder or projection head. Let $\theta$ represent the trainable parameters of this decoder model, which is typically a small neural network that maps from compressed representations to output predictions. As each example is presented, the model parameters are updated using gradient descent:
$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\big(g(z_i; \theta), y_i\big)
$$
The rule is the same gradient step once more, now applied to stored embeddings $z_i$ and a small head whose prediction is $g(z_i; \theta)$, rather than to raw inputs. Only the head's parameters $\theta$ change, so this is the head-only case of @eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory, and the encoder runs once per example when the embedding is stored rather than on every update. This bounds the trainable portion of the model, but feasibility still depends on the head's activations and optimizer state alongside the replay buffer and runtime reserves.

When replay storage rather than model compute binds, a device can go further and learn a dictionary of recurring sensor-trace patterns, storing each example as a few nonzero coefficients over that dictionary instead of as raw samples. A dataset of traces $\mathbf{X}$ then factorizes as $\mathbf{X} \approx \mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{dict}}\mathbf{C}$, where the columns of $\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{dict}}$ are the basis patterns and the block-sparse coefficient matrix $\mathbf{C}$ records which patterns are active in each example. The saving is real only if the dictionary plus all stored coefficients is smaller than the raw replay examples, and updating the dictionary changes the representation of every stored example, so reconstruction quality and compatibility become part of the replay policy.

Compressed representations can reduce how long raw inputs remain stored, but an embedding is not anonymized merely because it is lower dimensional. It may preserve identity, attributes, or enough structure for inversion, and it must receive the same access-control, retention, and deletion analysis as the source data unless a separate privacy mechanism establishes a stronger guarantee. Compression can also act as an implicit regularizer, smoothing learning and mitigating overfitting when only a few training examples are available.

In keyword spotting, raw audio can first be transformed into mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs),[^fn-mfcc-audio-compression] a compact, lossy representation derived from the speech power spectrum. Storing these vectors instead of waveforms reduces the replay payload. The complete adaptation budget must still include feature extraction, model state, and the working memory needed for updates.

[^fn-mfcc-audio-compression]: **MFCCs (Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients)**\index{Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients!definition}: For a 320-sample audio window (20 ms at 16 kHz), 16-bit samples occupy 640 bytes, while 12--13 coefficients stored at 32 bits each occupy approximately 50 bytes. The roughly 13$\times$ reduction compares one waveform window with one feature vector; overlapping windows, additional features, and metadata change the storage ratio for a complete recording. Replay capacity depends on that complete representation, and keyword detection quality must be evaluated separately from byte savings.

### Data efficiency strategy comparison {#sec-edge-intelligence-data-efficiency-strategy-comparison-4f92}

The choice of data-efficiency mechanism depends on what is scarce. Few-shot adaptation uses a small informative support set, replay spends memory and compute to preserve prior behavior, and compressed representations extend the history that fits on-device. Their limits remain different: weak pretrained features can defeat few-shot adaptation, a replay buffer can omit rare cases, and compression can discard task-relevant information. @Tbl-ondevice-techniques summarizes these on-device learning trade-offs\index{On-Device Learning!trade-offs}; combinations must fit the same memory, energy, and privacy budget.

| **Technique**                  |     **Data Requirements**     | **Memory/Compute Overhead** | **Use Case Fit**                                   |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:---------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------|
| **Few-Shot Adaptation**        | Small labeled set ($n_{\text{shot}}$ examples) |             Low             | Personalization, quick on-device finetuning        |
| **Experience Replay**          |         Streaming data        |  Moderate (buffer & update) | Non-stationary data, stability under drift         |
| **Compressed Representations** |   Unlabeled or encoded data   |       Low to Moderate       | Memory-limited devices; privacy-sensitive contexts |

: **On-Device Learning Trade-Offs**: Technique choice depends on the binding edge constraint: few-shot adaptation minimizes labeled-data needs, replay improves stability under drift at the cost of memory, and compressed representations extend retention when raw data is too large or too sensitive to keep. {#tbl-ondevice-techniques}

In practice, these methods are not mutually exclusive. Many real-world systems combine them to achieve robust, efficient adaptation. For example, a keyword spotting system may use compressed audio features (e.g., MFCCs), finetune a few parameters from a small support set, and maintain a replay buffer of past embeddings for continual refinement.

Efficient adaptation and data strategies establish how a single device can learn from its user. Sharing those gains requires another decision: whether local updates contain information useful to a common model and can be combined within communication and privacy constraints. Federated learning supplies that coordination protocol. Personal state can remain local when sharing would not improve the population objective, and privacy controls must separately limit what transmitted updates disclose.

## Federated Learning Algorithms {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-learning-6e7e}

The voice assistant of the chapter's opening, now deployed to millions of homes whose intermittently available devices contribute updates when local conditions permit, shows what local adaptation alone cannot do. One household pronounces "data" as "DAY-tuh" and another as "DA-tuh"; a third, a technical household, says "machine learning" every day, while a fourth never has. Local adaptation can specialize each model to its own household, but nothing it learns travels. If the fourth household starts using the phrase, its model must learn it from scratch, even though millions of other devices already handle it. Federation offers that transfer when the observations support a common objective. The system must decide which changes improve shared representations and which should remain personal, then evaluate whether aggregation helps the intended users.

Federated learning (definition \ref{dfn-edge-intelligence-federated-learning}) supplies that transfer while each device keeps its raw examples local. The approach turns data locality into one privacy control, not a complete privacy guarantee. A system must still treat gradients, model deltas, participation timing, device identifiers, and aggregate statistics as sensitive outputs because these signals can reveal information about local users [@kairouz2021; @zhu2019deep].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: federated-savings-notebook
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FEDERATED COMMUNICATION SAVINGS (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Model Updates vs Raw Data" .callout-notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Compare one compressed FL uplink round with one raw-data upload.
# │ Show: one-round uplink reduction ≈ 80x—inline in notebook result.
# │ How: Ratio = Data_Raw/Data_One_Model_Update.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_qty_int

class FederatedSavings:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_images = 1000  # Images collected by user per week
    img_size_kb = 200  # Compressed JPEG
    model_params_m = 5
    compression_ratio = 10  # Quantized updates (e.g., 4-bit)
    bits_per_update_param = 4  # 4-bit quantized updates
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    raw_data = n_images * img_size_kb * KB
    # Update size: 5M params * 4 bits / 8 bits-per-byte = 2.5 MB
    update = model_params_m * MILLION * bits_per_update_param / BITS_PER_BYTE * byte
    reduction = (raw_data / update).to_base_units().magnitude
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(70 < reduction < 90, f"Reduction {reduction:.1f}x unexpected")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    fs_raw_data_mb_str = fmt_qty_int(raw_data, MB, commas=False)
    fs_update_mb_str = fmt_memory(update, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    fs_reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(reduction, commas=False, precision=0)
```

For this camera-personalization scenario, one compact model-update uplink is much smaller than one upload of the week's raw observations. Total federated communication still depends on the number of rounds and on model downloads.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_edge_intelligence_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Violet network ladder comparing 200 MB of raw upload with a 2.5 MB federated update, with 80x marked as an annotation."}

*One compressed update is smaller than one raw-data upload; repeated rounds accumulate.*
:::

::: {#nbk-edge-intelligence-model-updates-vs-raw-data .callout-notebook title="Model updates vs. raw data"}

**Problem**: A team is designing a federated camera-personalization system that learns from `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_raw_data_mb_str` of compressed user images per week. Compare one upload of those images with one compressed model-update uplink round.

**Math**:
Bandwidth efficiency is the ratio of raw data volume to model update size.

1. **Raw data upload**\index{Raw Data Upload!definition}: `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_raw_data_mb_str`/week.
2. **One federated uplink round**\index{One Federated Uplink Round!definition}: A compressed model update (5M params) is `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_update_mb_str`.
3. **One-round uplink reduction**\index{One-Round Uplink Reduction!definition}: `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_raw_data_mb_str`/`{python} FederatedSavings.fs_update_mb_str` = `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_reduction_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: For this scenario, one `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_update_mb_str` uplink is `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_reduction_mult_str` smaller than one `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_raw_data_mb_str` raw-data upload. That ratio is not the end-to-end communication saving of a training run: after roughly `{python} FederatedSavings.fs_reduction_mult_str` uplink rounds, cumulative update uploads alone equal the raw-data volume, before counting global-model downloads, retries, or protocol overhead. The verdict therefore turns on the round schedule. A deployment that runs one round per day uploads seven updates per week of data, far below the break-even count, and saves most of the uplink traffic; one that runs a round every hour uploads 168 updates per week, more than the break-even count, and moves more bytes than shipping the images would. Per-round traffic must be multiplied by the expected round count before federation can claim a bandwidth saving.

:::

Across the three network topologies partitioned in @fig-centralized-vs-decentralized, federated learning\index{Edge Learning!paradigm} is the sole paradigm that aggregates fleet-wide experience across users without allowing raw training data to cross the device perimeter. Centralized-cloud training shares learning only by moving the data, and local-only adaptation keeps each insight on the device that found it, so one household's rare vocabulary never helps another. Federated learning buys that middle position with a protocol, and the rest of this section determines when the protocol yields a better shared model.

### Privacy-preserving collaborative learning {#sec-edge-intelligence-privacypreserving-collaborative-learning-ecf9}

Federated learning (FL) coordinates local training through shared-model updates [@mcmahan2017communication]. Its protocol must specify how heterogeneous clients contribute, how non-i.i.d. data distributions\index{Federated Learning!non-IID data challenges} affect local work, and which state remains personal. Secure aggregation and differential privacy impose additional constraints on what the coordinator may observe and how much noise the learning loop must absorb.

The first architectural decision is whether the participants form a cross-device or cross-silo federation. The voice assistant is cross-device, with millions of unreliable phones. A group of hospitals that want to train a complication-prediction model, but whose governance policies prohibit centralizing patient records, is cross-silo, with a few reliable institutions that each hold a large dataset. The distinction changes the failure model, scheduling policy, and privacy unit before any optimizer is selected (@tbl-edge-cross-device-silo) [@kairouz2021].

| **Design dimension**  | **Cross-device federation**                                     | **Cross-silo federation**                                                      |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Participants**      | Large population of intermittently available personal devices   | Small set of known organizations or sites                                      |
| **Round semantics**   | Sample an eligible cohort; expect stragglers and dropouts       | Coordinate a stable membership; investigate missing sites                      |
| **Trust boundary**    | Treat client software and local data as potentially compromised | Authenticate institutions, but still isolate each data custodian               |
| **Weighting default** | Decide whether the objective represents examples or users       | Weighting follows the agreed institutional objective, not site size by default |
| **Privacy unit**      | Usually a user or device across its participation history       | Usually a person or record within a site's data, sometimes the site itself     |

: **Cross-Device and Cross-Silo Federated Learning**: The participant population determines scheduling, trust, weighting, and privacy semantics. A protocol designed for millions of unreliable phones is not automatically appropriate for a consortium of hospitals. {#tbl-edge-cross-device-silo tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

### Learning protocols {#sec-edge-intelligence-learning-protocols-139a}

The protocols that make distributed coordination practical at scale must solve three engineering challenges simultaneously: ensuring that local training produces compatible updates despite non-IID data distributions, aggregating those updates efficiently despite bandwidth constraints, and coordinating timing across devices with heterogeneous availability patterns.

#### Local training {#sec-edge-intelligence-local-training-e73d}

Local training turns the device's adaptation policy into a contribution to a shared model. Every contribution needs a known starting version, a compatible parameter schema, and a declared local update rule. Otherwise, arrays with the same shape may describe changes to different models. The following synchronous protocol starts participating clients from the same shared version and keeps personal parameters outside the aggregate:

1. **Model initialization**\index{Model Initialization!definition}: Each device initializes its local model parameters, often by downloading the latest global model from the server.
2. **Local data sampling**\index{Local Data Sampling!definition}: The device samples a subset of its local data for training. This data may be non-IID, meaning that it may not be uniformly distributed across devices.
3. **Local training**\index{Local Training!definition}: The device performs a number of training iterations on its local data, updating the model parameters based on the computed gradients.
4. **Model update**\index{Model Update!definition}: After local training, the device computes a model update (e.g., the difference between the updated and initial parameters) and prepares to send it to the server.
5. **Update transmission**\index{Update Transmission!definition}: The device transmits the model update to the server, typically using a secure communication channel to protect user privacy.
6. **Model aggregation**\index{Model Aggregation!definition}: The server aggregates the updates from multiple devices to produce a new global model, which is then distributed back to the participating devices.

The process repeats with a new shared version for each accepted round. Update frequency depends on device availability, local work, and communication cost. A secure transmission channel protects the transfer, but the receiving server can still inspect the update unless the aggregation protocol separately hides individual contributions. Model compatibility and update confidentiality are therefore distinct protocol obligations.

#### Federated aggregation protocols {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-aggregation-protocols-5d37}

The central coordination mechanism in federated learning allows devices with small, local datasets to collaboratively train a shared model. Client devices perform local training and transmit model updates to a central server, which aggregates them into a refined global model and redistributes it for the next training round. The cyclical procedure decouples learning from centralized data collection, suiting environments where user data is private, bandwidth is constrained, and device participation is sporadic.

The most widely used baseline for this process is federated averaging (FedAvg),\index{FedAvg!definition} which has become a canonical algorithm for federated learning [@mcmahan2017communication]. In FedAvg, each device trains its local copy of the model using SGD on its private data. The algorithm is local SGD, which synchronizes only after several local steps to save communication, run with two changes that the data center version never faces. Only a sampled subset of clients participates in each round, and each client's data is a non-IID shard of the population, so the local steps that save communication also pull each client toward its own optimum.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Local SGD and the trade-off between synchronization frequency and convergence that it exposes are established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-distributed-training-efficiency-metrics-9488.
:::

Formally, let $\mathcal{D}_k$ denote the local dataset on client $k$, and let $\theta_k^t$ be the parameters of the model on client $k$ at round $t$. Each client performs $E$ epochs of SGD on its local data, yielding an update $\theta_k^{t+1}$. The central server then aggregates these updates as:
$$
\theta^{t+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{C} \frac{n_k}{n} \theta_k^{t+1}
$$ {#eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation}
where $n_k = |\mathcal{D}_k|$ is the number of samples on device $k$, $n = \sum_k n_k$ is the total number of samples across participating clients, and $C$ is the number of active devices in the current round. Here $C$ is a client count, unrelated to the C³ axes, and bare $E$ counts local epochs; the energy quantities of @eq-edge-background-admission always carry a subscript.

This formula optimizes an *example-weighted* objective: a client with ten times as many local examples receives ten times the influence. That choice is appropriate when every example should contribute equally, but it can let prolific users or large institutions dominate the model. A *user-weighted* objective instead assigns each participating client weight $1/C$, optionally capping or normalizing each client's local contribution before aggregation. Neither choice is universally fair. The system must declare whether its unit of interest is an example, a user, an organization, or a deployment cohort, then evaluate that population rather than inherit $n_k/n$ as an implementation default.

A deployed round wraps the averaging rule in policy that the equation leaves unstated (@fig-federated-averaging-cycle)\index{FedAvg!coordination cycle}. @Eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation fixes how completed models combine, but not which clients are invited, how long the coordinator waits, or how few completions force a round to be abandoned. Those protocol choices decide which contributions enter the sum. A client that misses the deadline contributes nothing, and its examples are absent from $n$ for that round. Over-selection and its population-coverage trade-off are developed in @sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675.

::: {#fig-federated-averaging-cycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Federated averaging protocol**: One FedAvg round in four steps. (1) The coordinator selects a cohort, over-selecting to absorb dropouts, and broadcasts the global model $\theta^t$. (2) Each client runs $E$ local epochs on its private data. (3) Clients that finish before the round deadline upload $\theta_k^{t+1}$; a straggler that misses the deadline is dropped. (4) The coordinator forms the example-weighted average of @eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation, which becomes the next global model." fig-alt="A coordinator box at the top holds step 1, select cohort and broadcast theta t, and step 4, aggregate theta t plus 1 as a sum of n k over n times theta k. A gray downlink bus delivers theta t to five client boxes below. Clients 1 to 4 each hold private data and run E local epochs, and send amber uploads through step 3 back to the aggregate step. Client 5 is a red dashed straggler that misses the deadline, with its upload marked by a cross. Step 2 is labeled local training on private data."}
![](images/svg/federated-averaging-cycle.svg)

:::

This basic structure introduces a number of design choices and trade-offs. The number of local epochs $E$ impacts the balance between computation and communication: larger $E$ reduces communication frequency but risks divergence if local data distributions vary too much. The selection of participating clients affects convergence stability and fairness. In real-world deployments, not all devices are available at all times, and hardware capabilities may differ substantially, requiring robust participation scheduling and failure tolerance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Federated rounds over intermittent wide-area clients contrast with the synchronous AllReduce collectives on low-latency cluster fabrics established in @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-allreduce-algorithms-7545.
:::

#### Time to target under client drift {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-learning-convergence-analysis-c1fc}

A federated deployment must reach a quality target within its time, energy, and participation budgets. More local training can reduce how often clients communicate, but it also changes their updates and the time each selected cohort takes to finish. The engineering comparison is therefore time to an agreed quality target, not communication rounds alone.

##### What the FedAvg controls count {#sec-edge-intelligence-convergence-rate-fundamentals-bfef}

FedAvg exposes the number of participating clients $C$, local epochs $E$, and communication rounds $R$ as controls [@mcmahan2017communication]. Their product $CER$ counts client-epochs when participation is fixed, which makes it the work ledger of a run rather than a measure of its progress. Clients can have different dataset sizes, and equal client-epoch counts can process different examples or produce conflicting updates, so two runs with the same $CER$ can end at very different quality. A convergence result is useful only when its assumptions match the optimizer, client sampling, and data distributions.

##### Non-IID data impact {#sec-edge-intelligence-noniid-data-impact-d8b9}

Non-IID data\index{Non-IID data!convergence impact} is where federated averaging departs from the data center version of local SGD. Each local step moves a client toward the optimum of its own shard, so after many local steps the client models sit near different optima, and their weighted average lands at a point that need not minimize the population objective. This client drift\index{Client Drift!federated learning} grows with the number of local steps and with how far the client distributions differ, and it degrades federated averaging relative to i.i.d. baselines [@li2020; @zhao2018federated]. It therefore eats into the benefit of fewer communications exactly where communication is most expensive. How strongly depends on the partition, update rule, participation policy, and local step size, and no universal heterogeneity score predicts a round count across applications, which is why @sec-edge-intelligence-quantifying-heterogeneity-practice-eece measures the trade-off rather than computing it.

##### Measuring the local-work trade-off {#sec-edge-intelligence-quantifying-heterogeneity-practice-eece}

Compare candidate local-epoch settings under the same initialization, data partition, participation policy, and held-out quality target. For each setting $E$, record the first validated round $R(E)$ that reaches the target and the elapsed duration $t_r(E)$ of each completed round, including client selection, local work, transfer, aggregation, and any waiting. The observed time to target is

$$
T_{\text{target}}(E) = \sum_{r=1}^{R(E)} t_r(E).
$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Time to target — communication term of one federated round.
# │ Scope: local — reference adapter payload over a constrained mobile uplink.
from mlsysim import ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.core.units import minute, second, ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_time

class EdgeRoundUploadTime:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    adapter_update = ReferenceStats.EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.FederatedLoraUpdate
    uplink_low = 1 * ureg.megabit / second  # scenario assumption: constrained uplink of the federated-design checkpoint
    uplink_high = 10 * ureg.megabit / second  # scenario assumption: same checkpoint range, upper end
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    upload_slow = (adapter_update / uplink_low).to(second)
    upload_fast = (adapter_update / uplink_high).to(second)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(6 < upload_slow.to(minute).magnitude < 8, f"Slow upload drifted: {upload_slow}")
    check(35 < upload_fast.magnitude < 50, f"Fast upload drifted: {upload_fast}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    upload_slow_min_str = fmt_time(round(upload_slow.to(minute).magnitude) * minute, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    upload_fast_s_str = fmt_time(round(upload_fast.magnitude) * second, second, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
```

Each $t_r(E)$ is one instance of the round budget sketched at the opening of the chapter. Read through the Fleet Law, it is the local training on the slowest client the round still awaits, plus the upload, plus the wait for enough reports, less whatever overlaps. The communication piece is easy to estimate. Over a constrained mobile uplink of 1 to 10 Mbps, the chapter's reference adapter update of `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.federated_lora_update_mb_str` takes about `{python} EdgeRoundUploadTime.upload_slow_min_str` to upload at the low end and about `{python} EdgeRoundUploadTime.upload_fast_s_str` at the high end, and that cost recurs in every one of the $R(E)$ rounds. A setting of $E$ that halves $R(E)$ therefore removes half of the cumulative upload time, and it pays off only if the extra local training it adds to each round, on the slowest awaited client, costs less than the uploads it removes. Client drift keeps that comparison from being settled on paper, because more local steps can also raise $R(E)$, and only the measured ledger below can rank the settings.

A useful experiment ledger records local epochs, completed clients, rounds to target, elapsed time, transmitted bytes, and device energy. If a run never reaches the quality target within the budget, report that outcome rather than extrapolating an invented convergence curve. Repeated runs and cohort-level validation distinguish a stable improvement from a fortunate sample of participating devices.

##### Communication-computation trade-off {#sec-edge-intelligence-communicationcomputation-tradeoff-6e31}

@Fig-comm-compute-tradeoff diagrams the opposing systems paths governed by local work $E$: increasing local epochs lengthens per-round execution duration $t_r(E)$ (the upper branch) while reducing synchronization frequency (the lower branch), which can lower the required rounds $R(E)$ until client drift penalizes convergence. Both paths merge into the cumulative time to target $T_{\text{target}}(E)$, which remains admissible only if total consumption fits within client energy and fleet-coverage budgets. A setting that requires fewer rounds can still prolong total wall-clock duration. Selecting $E$ therefore requires evaluating an empirical ledger alongside physical admission constraints, rather than relying on ungrounded heuristics.

::: {#fig-comm-compute-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Measuring the local-work trade-off**: The local-work setting $E$ acts through two opposing paths. More local epochs lengthen each round, $t_r(E)$, while reducing how often clients synchronize, which can lower the rounds to target, $R(E)$, unless client drift raises it. Only their combination, the measured time to target $T_{\text{target}}(E)$, ranks candidate settings, and a setting is admissible only if it also fits the client energy and population-coverage budgets." fig-alt="A violet box for local work, E epochs, branches to a blue box, round duration t r of E, grows with E, and an amber box, rounds to target R of E, fewer syncs, more drift. Both feed a box, time to target T target of E equals the sum of t r of E over R of E rounds, which connects to a dashed box, within energy and coverage budgets."}
![](images/svg/federated-round-ledger.svg)
:::

The operating point depends on the deployment. Larger local updates can amortize transfer overhead, but they also change drift, completion time, and which clients finish. The network alone can move the optimum, as a cost model in relative units shows (@fig-fl-communication-computation). Its minimum $E^*$ shifts from $E=10$ on the fast-network curve to $E=40$ on the slow-network curve because amortizing expensive transfers justifies more local work. These curves are not measured convergence results. A deployment must establish whether additional local work actually reduces time to target after drift and client completion are counted, and adaptive epoch policies need the same outcome and coverage checks as fixed settings.

::: {#fig-fl-communication-computation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning**: As network bandwidth decreases from fast to slow, the time-minimizing number of local epochs shifts rightward because additional local computation amortizes more communication. The curves come from an illustrative cost model in relative units, not measurements; its growing local-work term stands in for the longer rounds and added drift that make excessive local work counterproductive." fig-alt="Three curves of total training time vs. local epochs for fast, medium, and slow networks. Optimal points shift right as bandwidth decreases."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FL COMMUNICATION-COMPUTATION (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-fl-communication-computation—federated learning trade-off
# │
# │ Goal: Plot total time vs local epochs E for Fast/Medium/Slow network; show
# │       optimal E shifts right as bandwidth decreases.
# │ Show: Three curves; optimal points; annotation.
# │ How: y = comm_cost/E + compute_cost*E + overhead; argmin; matplotlib.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Plot total time vs local epochs E for Fast/Medium/Slow network; show
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
import numpy as np

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8.5, 4.8))

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
E = np.linspace(1, 50, 200)

y_fast = (100 / E) + (1.0 * E) + 5
y_fast = y_fast * 0.1

y_med = (400 / E) + (1.0 * E) + 5
y_med = y_med * 0.12

y_slow = (1600 / E) + (1.0 * E) + 5
y_slow = y_slow * 0.15

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.plot(E, y_fast, label='Fast network', color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=2.3)
ax.plot(E, y_med, label='Medium network', color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], linewidth=2.3)
ax.plot(E, y_slow, label='Slow network', color=COLORS['RedLine'], linewidth=2.3)

opt_fast_idx = np.argmin(y_fast)
opt_med_idx = np.argmin(y_med)
opt_slow_idx = np.argmin(y_slow)

ax.scatter(E[opt_fast_idx], y_fast[opt_fast_idx], color=COLORS['GreenLine'], s=80, zorder=5, edgecolor='white')
ax.scatter(E[opt_med_idx], y_med[opt_med_idx], color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], s=80, zorder=5, edgecolor='white')
ax.scatter(E[opt_slow_idx], y_slow[opt_slow_idx], color=COLORS['RedLine'], s=80, zorder=5, edgecolor='white')

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.annotate(
    'Optimal local work ($E$)\nincreases as network slows',
    xy=(E[opt_slow_idx], y_slow[opt_slow_idx] + 2),
    xytext=(28, 50),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", connectionstyle="arc3, rad=-0.2", color=COLORS['primary'], shrinkB=5, relpos=(1.0, 0.5), lw=0.9),
    fontsize=8.5,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=COLORS['primary'],
    ha='center',
    va='center',
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', fc='white', ec='#CBD5E1', lw=0.9),
)

ax.set_xlabel('Local Epochs per Round ($E$)')
ax.set_ylabel('Total Training Time (relative units, log scale)')
ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_ylim(1, max(y_slow) * 1.5)

ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8, frameon=True, facecolor='white', framealpha=0.95, edgecolor='#CBD5E1')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

##### Diagnosing a missed target {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-learning-work-93a2}

Federated convergence results depend on the update rule, objective, sampling policy, and assumptions about client data [@kairouz2021]. Heterogeneity, participation, and local sample counts are therefore inputs to a feasibility assessment, not universal pass/fail thresholds. A deployment must demonstrate that its chosen configuration reaches the declared quality target within time and device budgets, with evaluation that represents the intended population.

When a configuration misses that target, the measured failure guides the next experiment. Conflicting local updates motivate testing less local work, a different optimizer, or personalization. Long waits motivate scheduling or asynchronous alternatives, subject to privacy-protocol compatibility. Sparse local evidence motivates bounded adaptation and stronger validation. None of these changes replaces observations from absent cohorts; each must be reevaluated for quality, resource cost, and population coverage.

The aggregation rule specifies how compatible local models produce a shared model; the measured time-to-target ledger establishes whether a configuration reaches its objective within budget. A controlled lab can hold participant availability and network conditions steady. A phone fleet cannot, so the implementation must define how selection, deadlines, and failures change the set of updates that actually enters each aggregate. These protocol decisions connect learning behavior to fleet orchestration.

## Federated Learning Systems at Scale {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-systems}

A round selects a cohort from the deployment population, but some selected devices overheat, lose Wi-Fi, enter power-saving mode, or power off before returning an update. A fleet of millions of smartphones need not participate in one round for these failures to matter. The orchestrator must decide which clients are eligible, how long to wait, and what evidence permits aggregation when only part of the selected cohort completes.

### Client scheduling {#sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675}

Federated learning operates under the assumption that clients, or devices that hold local data, periodically become available for participation in training rounds. In real-world systems, client availability is intermittent and variable. Devices may be turned off, disconnected from power, lacking network access, or otherwise unable to participate at any given time. As a result, client scheduling\index{Client Scheduling!federated learning} plays a central role in the effectiveness and efficiency of distributed learning.

At a baseline level, federated ML systems define eligibility criteria for participation. A mobile deployment may require devices to be plugged in, connected to Wi-Fi, and idle to limit interference with foreground work and battery use. The chosen criteria determine which subset of the total population is considered "available" for a training round; they are deployment policy rather than requirements of federated learning itself.

Beyond these operational filters, devices also differ in their hardware capabilities, data availability, and network conditions. Some smartphones contain many recent examples relevant to the current task, while others have outdated or irrelevant data. Network bandwidth and upload speed may vary widely depending on geography and carrier infrastructure. As a result, uniform random selection from the eligible pool does not guarantee coverage of the full deployment population; eligibility has already excluded some devices and their data.

Availability-driven selection introduces participation bias\index{Participation Bias!federated learning}, the fleet-level consequence of the admission test in @eq-edge-background-admission (principle \ref{pri-participation-selects-population}). Clients with favorable conditions, such as frequent charging, high-end hardware, and consistent connectivity, pass admission and participate repeatedly, while others are systematically underrepresented. This can skew the resulting model toward behaviors and preferences of a privileged subset of the population, raising both fairness and generalization concerns.

Participation bias becomes severe when a small eligible cohort supplies most completed updates while other cohorts rarely participate. Completion logs and population coverage must establish the size of that skew in the actual deployment. This creates a feedback loop: models become more strongly optimized for users with high-end devices and stable connectivity, potentially degrading performance for resource-constrained users who need adaptation the most. A keyboard prediction model might become biased toward the typing patterns of users with flagship phones who charge overnight, missing important linguistic variations from users with budget devices or irregular charging patterns.

The order of these decisions limits what any remedy can do. Fleet orchestration admits only feasible allocations before a fairness policy divides them (principle \ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}), and a federated scheduler inherits the same order with a sharper consequence. Its eligibility filter fixes the candidate pool, so a fairness policy can redistribute rounds only among devices the admission test already accepted; a device that never qualifies is invisible to it.

Scheduling must therefore balance completion speed with population coverage. Stratified or quota-based sampling can prioritize underrepresented groups among eligible devices, while cumulative participation records can guide later invitations. Weighting methods require estimates of the population and selection process; they cannot recover observations from a cohort that never participates. Buffered asynchronous aggregation [@fedbuff], whose mechanism @sec-edge-intelligence-asynchronous-device-synchronization-348e describes, staleness-aware methods [@rodio2024], and fairness-oriented weighting [@fedstaleweight] offer additional controls. Their effectiveness must be checked through completed participation and cohort quality, rather than inferred from the scheduling rule alone.

These fairness mechanisms sit alongside adaptive client selection strategies. Federated ML systems can prioritize clients with underrepresented data types, target geographies or demographics that are less frequently sampled, and use historical participation data to enforce fairness constraints. Predictive modeling can anticipate later client availability or success rates, improving training throughput.

Selected clients perform one or more local training steps on their private data and transmit their model updates to a central server. These updates are aggregated to form a new global model. Typically, this aggregation is weighted, where the contributions of each client are scaled, for example, by the number of local examples used during training, before averaging. Example weighting gives larger local datasets more influence whether or not they represent the target population any better.

Scheduling must also bound how long a round waits on its slowest participants. Network latency, battery depletion, or background process contention can make some devices (stragglers) take 10$\times$ longer than the median, and the round cannot aggregate until enough updates arrive.

::: {.column-margin}
```{=latex}
\vspace*{-25mm}
```
![](images/svg/edge_intelligence_straggler_cutoff_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip showing the first K federated-client updates accepted before the round closes, while a late straggler is dropped."}

*Over-selection closes the round on the first K updates.*
:::

To prevent the global model update from stalling, production FL systems employ **over-selection**\index{Over-Selection!definition}. The server selects a candidate pool size $K_{\text{candidates}}$ larger than the target number of updates $K_{\text{target}}$ (the production system of @bonawitz2019towards selects about 130 percent of the target, $K_{\text{candidates}} \approx 1.3 \times K_{\text{target}}$). The server aggregates updates from the first $K_{\text{target}}$ responders and discards the rest. This approach bounds the round duration by the speed of the $K_{\text{target}}$-th fastest device rather than the absolute slowest. Accepting the fastest responders can amplify the participation bias just described, so shorter rounds must be evaluated against cohort coverage and wall-clock time to the declared quality target.

These scheduling decisions directly impact convergence rate, model generalization, energy consumption, and overall user experience. Poor scheduling results in excessive stragglers, overfitting to narrow client segments, or wasted computation. Client scheduling is therefore a core component of system design in federated learning, demanding both algorithmic insight and infrastructure-level coordination.

### Bandwidth-aware update compression {#sec-edge-intelligence-bandwidthaware-update-compression-7730}

Update compression\index{Communication efficiency!gradient compression} begins with a bottleneck diagnosis. Transmitting full weights or gradients can exhaust a client's transfer window or energy allowance before its update reaches the coordinator.[^fn-wireless-bandwidth-bottleneck] When transfer is limiting, the design decision is which information to quantize, sparsify, or keep local. The smaller payload must then be evaluated against encoding cost, update error, and the rounds required to reach the quality target.

[^fn-wireless-bandwidth-bottleneck]: **Wireless Upload Asymmetry**\index{Wireless Upload Asymmetry!definition}: Federated updates use the uplink, whose available throughput can differ substantially from the downlink and vary with coverage and contention. Transfer time depends on encoded update size and effective uplink goodput; energy also depends on radio state and transfer duration. Low-power links may add duty-cycle constraints. Compression is useful when these costs bind the update budget, but its necessity depends on the payload, link, and permitted synchronization interval.

The compression decision separates into three levers, each changing a different part of the communication bottleneck: model compression reduces bits per update, selective sharing reduces which parameters travel, and architectural partitioning keeps some state local. Model compression methods reduce the wire footprint of transmitted updates through quantization,\index{Gradient Quantization!definition} sparsification, or subsampling. Instead of sending full-precision gradients, a client transmits 8-bit quantized updates or communicates only the top-$k$ gradient elements[^fn-sparsification-topk-gradient] with highest magnitude, the same encodings that cluster training applies to its collective payloads. At the edge they bind in a different place. They act on a slow, asymmetric uplink rather than a fabric, under secure aggregation that must still combine the encoded updates, and inside a per-round communication ledger (@eq-edge-federated-communication-ledger) that also counts downloads and retries. These transformations are communication mechanisms, not privacy mechanisms; a smaller embedding, sparse update, or low-precision gradient may still expose membership, attributes, or reconstructable features.

[^fn-sparsification-topk-gradient]: **Gradient Sparsification**\index{Gradient Sparsification!definition}: Selecting the largest 1--10 percent of gradient elements by magnitude reduces transmitted value count by 10--100$\times$ before coordinate indices and other metadata are included. Sparsified SGD and deep gradient compression retain untransmitted residuals for later updates rather than assuming that small components can be discarded permanently [@stich2018sparsified; @lin2018deep]. Wire-byte savings depend on the encoding, while convergence depends on the residual handling, optimizer, and compression schedule; a value-count reduction alone establishes neither.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Gradient quantization, top-$k$ sparsification, and the error feedback that keeps compressed training convergent are established in @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-gradient-compression-7a5c.
:::

Selective update sharing further reduces communication by transmitting only subsets of model parameters or updates. In layer-wise selective sharing, clients update only certain layers, typically the final classifier or adapter modules, while keeping the majority of the backbone frozen. This reduces the update payload and limits which shared representations can change, but the trainable subset can still overfit nonrepresentative client data.

Architectural partitioning\index{Split learning!model partitioning}\index{Model partitioning!edge-cloud split} requires specifying what crosses the boundary. A personal/shared parameter partition keeps local modules private while aggregating selected shared parameters. Split learning instead divides execution between client and server, exchanging intermediate activations and backward gradients at the cut. These designs have different traffic and exposure patterns; neither guarantees a communication reduction or privacy merely by dividing the model.

These approaches can use the FedAvg aggregation protocol (@sec-edge-intelligence-federated-aggregation-protocols-5d37) only when their encoding and shared parameter schema support weighted aggregation. Quantization requires compatible scales, sparse updates require coordinate identities, and local-only parameters must stay outside the shared aggregate. With secure aggregation, the encoding must support combination without exposing individual decoded updates. The full communication ledger for round $r$ is

$$
M_r = M_{\text{download},r} + M_{\text{upload},r} + M_{\text{protocol},r} + M_{\text{retry},r},
$$ {#eq-edge-federated-communication-ledger}

@Eq-edge-federated-communication-ledger makes download, upload, protocol, and retry traffic explicit. The download distributes model state, the upload carries client updates, protocol traffic covers authentication and cryptographic setup, and retries account for failed or repeated transfers. Optimizing only $M_{\text{upload},r}$ can therefore move rather than remove the bottleneck. While amortizing network transfers through additional local computation relieves bandwidth pressure, alternative communication-efficient update strategies introduce their own systems trade-offs: compression may degrade gradient fidelity, selective updates can limit model capacity, and split architectures complicate coordination. Effective federated learning requires balancing communication, privacy, and convergence against the capabilities and variability of the client population.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The break-even condition under which encoding and decoding time costs less than the transfer time compression saves is developed, with a worked example, in @sec-appdx-comm-foundations-compression.
:::

The local-work schedule and update encoding jointly determine communication cost. @Fig-gradient-compression compares uncompressed 32-bit values (Panel A) with uniform 8-bit quantization (Panel B), which gives a $4\times$ reduction in value bytes before scales and other metadata are counted. Top-$k$ sparsification with retained error feedback (Panel C) must encode coordinate identities as well as selected values. Error feedback retains untransmitted residuals and adds local state. The receiving path must reconstruct or aggregate these encodings consistently, with separate compatibility requirements when secure aggregation hides individual updates.

::: {#fig-gradient-compression fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Gradient compression techniques**: Standard updates transmit full-precision values; quantization maps values to lower-precision buckets, such as FP32 to INT8; and sparsification transmits only the most significant top-$k$ gradients. The latter two mechanisms reduce bytes transferred but introduce representation error or residual state that the training algorithm must manage." fig-alt="Three-panel comparison of gradient vector representations: standard FP32, quantized INT8, and sparsified Top-k with arrows to server."}
