:::

Compression is useful when its reduction in total communication outweighs encoding work and any extra rounds needed to reach the quality target. A smaller upload helps a round only if transfer was what made clients miss the deadline or excluded a cohort, and the round's completion logs show which. Even when transfer becomes feasible, the shared model may still fail to capture local variation.

### Federated personalization {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-personalization-3c73}

Devices can complete compatible updates yet disagree about which behavior improves their local task. A shared model may serve that population adequately, or its aggregate gain may conceal persistent losses for particular users. Personalized federated learning\index{Personalized federated learning!objective} retains shared learning while allowing selected parameters or models to specialize. Its value must be evaluated against the added local state, training cost, and risk of overfitting sparse user data.

Let $\theta_k$ denote the model parameters on client $k$, and $\theta_{\text{global}}$ the aggregated global model. For $C$ clients, counted as in @eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation, traditional FL seeks to minimize a global objective:
$$
\min_\theta \sum_{k=1}^{C} w_k \mathcal{L}_k(\theta)
$$
where $\mathcal{L}_k(\theta)$ is the local loss on client $k$, and $w_k$ is a weighting factor (e.g., proportional to local dataset size). This formulation optimizes the weighted average loss of a shared model $\theta$; it does not guarantee acceptable performance for every client. Local loss landscapes $\mathcal{L}_k$ can differ across clients, reflecting non-IID data distributions and varying task requirements.

Personalization modifies this objective to allow each client to maintain its own adapted parameters $\theta_k$, optimized with respect to both the global model and local data:
$$
\min_{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_C} \sum_{k=1}^{C} \left( \mathcal{L}_k(\theta_k) + \lambda_{\text{reg}} \cdot \mathcal{R}(\theta_k, \theta_{\text{global}}) \right)
$$

Here, $\mathcal{R}$ penalizes deviation from the global model, and $\lambda_{\text{reg}}$ controls the strength of that penalty. The displayed objective describes local specialization around a given global reference; a complete protocol must additionally specify how that reference is trained and refreshed. The penalty trades local fit against proximity to the shared model, without guaranteeing improvement for every client.

Real-world use cases illustrate the importance of this approach. Consider a wearable health monitor that tracks physiological signals to classify physical activities. While a global model may perform reasonably well across the population, individual users exhibit different motion patterns, gait signatures, or sensor placements. Finetuning the final classification layer or low-rank adapters provides a way to address these differences. Evaluation must establish whether the local examples support an improvement, especially for rare classes with little supervision.

Several personalization strategies address the trade-offs between compute overhead, information exposure, and adaptation speed. One widely used approach is local finetuning, in which each client downloads the latest global model and performs a small number of gradient steps using its local data. This method avoids transmitting those examples during adaptation, but the resulting local state and any later update remain privacy-sensitive. It may also yield suboptimal results when the global model is poorly aligned with the client's data distribution or when the local dataset is extremely limited.

Another effective technique involves personalization layers, where the model is partitioned\index{Model partitioning!personalization layers}\index{Split learning!personalization layers} into a shared backbone and a lightweight, client-specific head, typically the final classification layer [@arivazhagan2019federated]. In FedPer, clients train both the shared base and their personal head, but only the shared base participates in server aggregation; the head remains local. A separate head-only adaptation policy can freeze a downloaded backbone to reduce local training cost when the relevant variation lies mainly in output categories or decision boundaries.

Clustered federated learning\index{Clustered federated learning!client grouping} offers an alternative by grouping clients according to similarities in their data or performance characteristics, and training separate models for each cluster. This strategy can enhance accuracy within homogeneous subpopulations but introduces additional system complexity and may require exchanging metadata to determine group membership.

Finally, meta-learning approaches, such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML),[^fn-maml-fewshot-adaptation] aim to produce a global model initialization that can be quickly adapted to new tasks with just a few local updates [@finn2017model]. This technique is especially useful when clients have limited data or operate in environments with frequent distributional shifts.

[^fn-maml-fewshot-adaptation]: **MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning)**\index{MAML!definition}: @finn2017model optimize for a model initialization from which one or a few gradient steps can yield good performance on a new task, with experiments including one-shot and few-shot settings. Meta-training is more expensive than ordinary finetuning because it differentiates through the adaptation process, but deployment adaptation can be limited to a small number of local updates. This makes MAML relevant for edge scenarios where inference compute is cheap but training data is scarce.

Each strategy occupies a different point in the personalization trade-off space\index{Personalization!trade-offs}. @Tbl-personalization-strategies compares compute overhead, information exposure, and adaptation latency across local finetuning, personalization layers\index{Personalization layer!trade-offs}, clustered federated learning, and meta-learning. The mechanism determines what state is shared; a privacy guarantee requires separately specified controls and assumptions.

| **Strategy**               | **Personalization Mechanism**                     |  **Compute Overhead** |               **Privacy** **Preservation**               |   **Adaptation Speed**  |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:---------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **Local Finetuning**       | Gradient descent on local loss postaggregation    |    Low to Moderate    | Raw examples stay local; adapted state remains sensitive |     Fast (few steps)    |
| **Personalization Layers** | Split model: shared base + user-specific head     |        Moderate       |     Narrows shared state; does not guarantee privacy     | Fast (train small head) |
| **Clustered FL**           | Group clients by data similarity, train per group |    Moderate to High   |     Group membership and updates can leak attributes     |          Medium         |
| **Meta-Learning**          | Train for fast adaptation across tasks/devices    | High (meta-objective) |     Depends on meta-training and adaptation protocol     |   Very Fast (few-shot)  |

: **Personalization Trade-Offs**: Federated learning strategies balance personalization with compute, information exposure, and adaptation latency. Data locality narrows exposure but does not by itself provide a privacy guarantee. {#tbl-personalization-strategies}

Selecting an on-device personalization strategy requires balancing adaptation capacity against memory residency. @Fig-personalization-arch contrasts the structural footprint of three fine-tuning paradigms: full fine-tuning of every backbone layer (Column A), head-only adaptation that freezes feature extractors (Column B), and parameter-efficient adapters inserted alongside frozen backbone blocks (Column C).

::: {#fig-personalization-arch fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Federated personalization architectures**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every layer; (B) head-only adaptation freezes the feature extractor and trains only the task head; (C) adapter-based learning, such as LoRA, inserts small trainable modules beside a frozen backbone. The dashed arrow marks how far the backward pass must reach. Adapters shrink trainable state, but because they sit at every depth their gradients still traverse the backbone, so the required backward state must be retained or recomputed. In this comparison, head-only adaptation truncates the backward pass at the feature extractor." fig-alt="Three columns of four layer boxes above a task head. Column A: all layers and the head are blue and trainable, with a dashed backward arrow spanning the whole column. Column B: layers are gray and frozen, the head is blue, and a short dashed arrow spans only the head. Column C: layers are gray and frozen with a small blue adapter box beside each, the head is blue, and the dashed arrow spans the whole column. A legend marks gray as frozen, blue as trainable, and the dashed arrow as backward pass extent."}
![](images/svg/personalization-arch.svg)

:::

The dashed backward-pass arrows in @fig-personalization-arch are the activation term of @eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory drawn as distance. Adapters at early layers in Column C pull the backward path through the later backbone, whose saved state must be retained or recomputed, while head-only adaptation in Column B ends it at the head, as in the wake-word case of @sec-edge-intelligence-fewshot-learning-data-streaming-566e. Placement sets the dependency path, and the execution schedule sets how much of that state stays resident.

### Federated privacy {#sec-edge-intelligence-federated-privacy-a1ed}

While federated learning is often motivated by privacy concerns, as it involves keeping raw data localized instead of transmitting it to a central server, the paradigm introduces its own set of security and privacy risks. Although devices do not share their raw data, the transmitted model updates (such as gradients or weight changes) can inadvertently leak information about the underlying private data. Techniques such as model inversion attacks[^fn-inversion-edge-training] and membership inference attacks\index{Membership Inference Attack!definition}\index{Membership Inference!privacy risk} demonstrate that adversaries may partially reconstruct or infer properties of local datasets by analyzing these updates.

[^fn-inversion-edge-training]: **Model Inversion Attack**\index{Model Inversion Attack!definition}\index{Model Inversion!federated attack}: Reconstructs training data from model outputs or gradients by optimizing inputs that maximize confidence scores [@fredrikson2015; @zhu2019deep]. In federated learning, gradient updates can leak more information than model outputs alone because they expose training-step information directly. Defenses such as gradient perturbation, secure aggregation, and differential privacy add protocol, utility, communication, or compute trade-offs whose magnitude depends on the threat model and deployment.

To mitigate such risks, federated ML systems can employ protective measures. **Secure aggregation**\index{Secure Aggregation!definition}[^fn-secagg-secure-aggregation] protocols reveal a combined result while hiding individual updates beyond what that result itself reveals, subject to the protocol's assumptions about collusion and participating clients. Differential Privacy\index{Differential Privacy!noise injection}\index{Differential Privacy!edge devices} techniques calibrate noise to bounded contributions to limit the effect of a protected user's or record's inclusion on the released result. The deployment must specify which unit receives that protection.

[^fn-secagg-secure-aggregation]: **Secure Aggregation**\index{Secure Aggregation!secret sharing protocol}: Cryptographic protocol where client pairs exchange random masks that cancel in the server-side sum, revealing only the aggregate gradient without exposing individual contributions [@bonawitz2017]. Production-scale federated systems such as Gboard combine secure aggregation with eligibility checks, drop-out handling, and round scheduling [@bonawitz2019towards]. The communication expansion and minimum-participation requirements depend on protocol parameters and the security model, so aggregation systems must wait for enough eligible devices before releasing a round.

These controls solve different problems. Secure aggregation limits what the coordinator learns about each submitted update, whereas differential privacy bounds how much a declared privacy unit can affect a released result. A deployment therefore needs a privacy ledger\index{Differential Privacy!privacy ledger and accounting} that records the unit of protection, clipping rule, noise mechanism, sampling assumptions, $(\epsilon,\delta)$ expenditure for every release, and cumulative composition across training and federated analytics [@abadi2016deep; @kairouz2021]. Clipping bounds each contribution before noise is calibrated. The parameters $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ describe the permitted change in output probabilities when the protected user or record is included or removed; composition accounts for repeated releases involving that unit. Resetting a round counter does not reset privacy loss for a user who participates again.

Secure aggregation also creates a robustness conflict. Byzantine-resilient rules\index{Secure Aggregation!Byzantine resilience conflict} such as Krum, coordinate-wise filtering, or per-client anomaly inspection need access to individual updates, while secure aggregation deliberately hides those updates [@blanchard2017machine; @bonawitz2017]. A system cannot claim both arbitrary per-client inspection and conventional secure aggregation over the same messages. It must instead validate clients before masking, use attested execution and bounded local updates, compute only aggregation-compatible checks, or adopt a protocol designed to evaluate approved robust statistics without revealing raw client contributions. @Fig-secure-agg models this cryptographic boundary through pairwise zero-sum masking: Clients A and B negotiate a shared random mask $r$ via Diffie-Hellman key agreement, perturbing their local updates into pseudo-random vectors ($y_A = \Delta\theta_A + r$ and $y_B = \Delta\theta_B - r$) before crossing into the server domain. When the aggregation server sums the received vectors, the symmetric masks cancel ($r - r = 0$), yielding the exact unmasked aggregate $\Delta\theta_A + \Delta\theta_B$. This two-client illustration assumes both clients complete the exchange and neither reveals its mask to the server. It demonstrates cancellation, not a complete protocol for collusion resistance or dropout recovery.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Byzantine failures, in which a worker stays alive but returns wrong results, and aggregation rules such as Krum and trimmed mean that bound their influence are established in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-byzantine-failures-8a24.
:::

::: {#fig-secure-agg fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Secure aggregation protocol**: A simplified two-client view of pairwise masking. Clients A and B agree on a shared random mask $r$; A uploads $y_A = \Delta\theta_A + r$ and B uploads $y_B = \Delta\theta_B - r$, so each upload alone looks random to the server. Summing them cancels the mask and yields exactly $\Delta\theta_A + \Delta\theta_B$. The server learns only the aggregate, which can still leak information unless differential privacy bounds it." fig-alt="Two client boxes on the left. In Client A, update delta theta A passes through a plus r node to produce y A; in Client B, update delta theta B passes through a minus r node to produce y B. A dashed line labeled shared mask r, key agreement, links the two mask nodes. Amber uplink arrows cross a dashed boundary from on device to visible to server, entering an aggregation server where a sum block produces delta theta A plus delta theta B, labeled masks cancel, r minus r equals 0."}
![](images/svg/secure-agg.svg)

:::

Secure aggregation and differential privacy\index{Differential Privacy!composition with secure aggregation} can protect different boundaries, but their composition must follow the threat model. If a trusted server adds noise after receiving an exact aggregate, the privacy guarantee applies to the released noisy result; it does not hide that exact aggregate from the server. A protocol designed for distributed noise can instead let the server receive only a noisy aggregate. Clipping, noise calibration, dropout assumptions, and repeated-release accounting must match the chosen protocol. Neither mechanism establishes that local data or updates are trustworthy.

::: {#chk-edge-intelligence-federated-system-design .callout-checkpoint title="Federated system design"}

Consider architecting a federated learning system for a fleet of 10 million mobile devices. The data is highly non-IID (users have distinct, clustered typing patterns), and the network environment is constrained (1-10 Mbps). Before choosing optimizations for this scenario, classify the local bottlenecks and state which system constraint dominates each decision.

Consider three design decisions:

1.  Aggregation: Select plain FedAvg, reduced local epochs, or personalization/clustering for the non-IID population, and justify how the choice controls client drift.
2.  Privacy: Decide whether the deployment needs formal differential-privacy noise or whether secure aggregation and data minimization are sufficient for the stated threat model; using the clipping and noise described in this section, explain why adding noise typically increases the rounds needed to reach the quality target.
3.  Communication: Choose between gradient quantization (e.g., 8-bit) and structured sparsity under constrained bandwidth, and justify the bandwidth/accuracy trade-off.

:::

### Large-scale device orchestration {#sec-edge-intelligence-largescale-device-orchestration-1360}

A round that selects a million phones overnight will see some fraction overheat, lose connectivity, or be unplugged before they report, and a few may submit corrupted or deliberately malicious updates. Coordinating that population requires protocols that handle Byzantine clients, network partitions\index{Network partition!federated learning} that temporarily cut participants off, and constrained communication. These challenges differ from controlled data center training, where high-bandwidth networks and managed infrastructure narrow the trust and availability envelope.

#### Network and bandwidth optimization {#sec-edge-intelligence-network-bandwidth-optimization-53da}

The communication bottleneck\index{Communication efficiency!edge fleets} becomes a scalability constraint when transfers exceed the available connection windows or dominate round time. Quantifying the actual transfer requirements exposes the design constraints on model architectures, update compression strategies, and client participation policies that determine system viability.

The federated communication hierarchy reveals the severe bandwidth constraints under which distributed learning must operate. Full model synchronization can require tens to hundreds of megabytes per training round for common deep models, which is a poor fit for intermittent mobile uplinks. Federated-optimization work therefore studies communication reduction through structured updates, quantization, sparsification, and selective transmission [@konevcny2016federated; @mcmahan2017communication]. Practical deployments often push this further by transmitting only adapters, heads, or compressed update summaries rather than complete model states. Communication frequency introduces a critical trade-off between model update freshness, where more frequent updates enable faster adaptation to changing conditions, and network efficiency constraints that limit sustainable bandwidth consumption.

Network infrastructure constraints directly impact participation rates and overall system viability. Mobile upload capacity varies sharply by geography, carrier, radio generation, congestion, and whether the device remains idle long enough to complete the transfer. A multi-megabyte update may be tolerable for a high-end device on a stable connection but impractical for a low-end device on a congested uplink. Communication policy must therefore balance completed updates against population coverage; optimizing only for fast connections can exclude the observations held by poorly connected clients.

Transfer size affects whether an eligible device can finish before its resource window closes. Smaller payloads can let clients with slower links complete, but the gain depends on whether transfer was the limiting cost. This communication efficiency\index{Communication efficiency!client participation rate} can improve population coverage without guaranteeing better model quality; compression error, weighting, and the data represented by newly completing clients still matter. Gradient quantization, sparsification, and top-$k$ selection with error accumulation (@sec-edge-intelligence-bandwidthaware-update-compression-7730) should therefore be evaluated by completed participation and cohort outcomes as well as bytes saved.

#### Asynchronous device synchronization {#sec-edge-intelligence-asynchronous-device-synchronization-348e}

Federated learning inherits failures from distributed systems and machine learning, but its coordination objective is not consensus, the problem of making replicated servers agree on one ordered log of operations. Federated clients agree on no such log. A coordinator instead decides which stochastic client updates are eligible, how stale updates are weighted, and which aggregation rule can tolerate faulty participants without letting them steer the model. Devices crash, lose power, or disconnect during rounds, while compromised clients can submit poisoned updates. Robust aggregation can reduce the influence of some faulty participants, but its assumptions, compute cost, and compatibility with secure aggregation must be explicit.

The trust chain begins before aggregation. A production coordinator authenticates the device and application instance, verifies the signed model and training-policy version, checks eligibility and freshness, binds the returned update to that version and round nonce, and records whether the update passed protocol-level bounds. Hardware-backed attestation can strengthen claims about code identity on supported devices, but it cannot prove that local examples are benign or representative. The resulting update-integrity record supports rejection, rollback, and incident analysis without treating device identity as evidence that the gradient is correct.

Network partitions pose particularly acute challenges for federated coordination protocols. Unlike traditional distributed systems operating within reliable data center networks, federated learning must gracefully handle prolonged client disconnection events where devices may remain offline for hours or days while traveling, in poor coverage areas, or simply powered down. Asynchronous coordination\index{Asynchronous coordination!federated learning} protocols enable continued training progress despite missing participants, but must carefully balance staleness (accepting potentially outdated contributions) against freshness (prioritizing recent but potentially sparse updates). Buffered asynchronous aggregation\index{Buffered asynchronous aggregation!mechanism} [@fedbuff] shows the mechanism. It removes the round barrier, letting each client train whenever its admission test passes and upload when done, while the server accumulates arriving updates in a buffer and applies their aggregate once a fixed number have arrived. Each update is down-weighted by its staleness, the number of server versions published since the client downloaded its starting model, so a slow client still contributes without dragging the shared model back toward an old state.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Gradient staleness, the delay between the model version a worker computed against and the version its update modifies, and its effect on convergence under bounded and fully asynchronous synchronization are established in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-staleness-impact-bsp-vs-ssp-vs-asp-e153.
:::

Recovery must distinguish coordinator state from device-local state. The coordinator checkpoints the global model and the optimizer and protocol state needed to resume accepted progress; this does not require a simultaneous checkpoint on every device. An incomplete round needs an explicit acceptance or abandonment rule, followed by evaluation of the population represented by its completed updates. State reconciliation\index{State reconciliation!offline clients} identifies a returning device's base version and determines which shared state it must download and which personal state remains compatible. Server-side load balancing can redistribute coordination work, but replacing an unavailable client with a faster one also changes the local data contributing to training.

The asynchronous nature of federated coordination introduces additional complexity in maintaining training convergence guarantees. Traditional synchronous training assumes all participants complete each round, but federated systems must handle stragglers[^fn-straggler-federated-delay] and dropouts gracefully.

[^fn-straggler-federated-delay]: **Straggler Problem**\index{Straggler Problem!definition}\index{Straggler!federated learning}: In data center training, stragglers slow synchronous progress; in federated learning, the problem is amplified by heterogeneous hardware, intermittent connectivity, and eligibility windows [@bonawitz2019towards; @kairouz2021]. Solutions like asynchronous aggregation and bounded staleness (ignoring updates computed against a model more than a fixed number of rounds old) improve throughput but introduce a fairness trade-off: aggressive straggler mitigation biases models toward users with high-end devices, potentially degrading performance for the most constrained users who need personalization most.

#### Heterogeneity management at fleet scale {#sec-edge-intelligence-managing-milliondevice-heterogeneity-86c1}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Federated heterogeneity — flagship NPU reference.
class EdgeFedNpuRecap:
    from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_multiple, fmt_ops_rate

    mobile_npu_rate = Hardware.Mobile.iPhone15Pro.compute.peak_flops
    mobile_npu_tops = mobile_npu_rate.to(TOPS).magnitude
    iot_tops = ReferenceStats.EdgeDeviceSpectrum.IotMicrocontrollerComputeLow
    compute_ratio = mobile_npu_tops / iot_tops.to(TOPS).magnitude
    check(1000 < compute_ratio < 2000, f"Flagship-to-IoT compute ratio unexpected: {compute_ratio:.0f}x")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    mobile_npu_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(mobile_npu_rate, unit=TOPS, precision=0, commas=False)
    iot_compute_tops_str = fmt_ops_rate(iot_tops, unit=TOPS, precision=2, commas=False)
    compute_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(compute_ratio, -2), precision=0, commas=True)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Federated heterogeneity energy constraints.
from mlsysim import ReferenceStats
from mlsysim.core.units import milliwatt, watt
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_qty_range

class EdgeFedPowerEnvelopeRecap:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    sustained_low = ReferenceStats.MobilePower.MobileMlSustainedLow
    sustained_high = ReferenceStats.MobilePower.MobileMlSustainedHigh
    background_low = ReferenceStats.MobilePower.BackgroundAdaptationLow
    background_high = ReferenceStats.MobilePower.BackgroundAdaptationHigh

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(sustained_low < sustained_high, "Sustained mobile power range should be ordered.")
    check(background_low < background_high, "Background mobile power range should be ordered.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    sustained_range_str = fmt_qty_range(
        sustained_low,
        sustained_high,
        watt,
        precision=0,
        commas=False,
    )
    background_range_str = fmt_qty_range(
        background_low,
        background_high,
        milliwatt,
        precision=0,
        commas=False,
    )
```

Million-device orchestration is a tiering decision: the system must decide which clients can train, which can only report lightweight updates, and how much bias that selection introduces. The difficulty is that hardware capabilities, network conditions, data distributions, and availability patterns vary simultaneously, challenging traditional distributed machine learning assumptions about homogeneous participants operating under similar conditions.

Real-world federated learning deployments face simultaneous variation in compute, memory, energy, and connectivity. The illustrative peak compute ratings differ by about `{python} EdgeFedNpuRecap.compute_ratio_mult_str` between flagship smartphones rated at `{python} EdgeFedNpuRecap.mobile_npu_tops_str` and, below Archetype C's phone-class clients, IoT microcontrollers rated at `{python} EdgeFedNpuRecap.iot_compute_tops_str`. These ratings do not translate into a training-speed ratio, because supported precision, backward operators, memory traffic, and sustained execution determine update time. Memory spans the same `{python} EdgeDeviceSpectrum.memory_ratio_mult_str` range from microcontroller SRAM to flagship phone RAM met in @sec-edge-intelligence-model-constraints-9232, and at fleet scale that range decides which update state each tier can retain at all. Energy budgets further restrict when that work can run. Background adaptation in this example targets roughly `{python} EdgeFedPowerEnvelopeRecap.background_range_str`, while phones may sustain `{python} EdgeFedPowerEnvelopeRecap.sustained_range_str` for foreground ML workloads and burst higher briefly. Network throughput, latency, and interruption patterns must likewise be measured for the participating clients before selecting update frequency and compression.

Tiered participation can assign different amounts of local work while preserving a compatible shared-update contract. A capable phone may complete more steps, while a constrained client contributes a smaller update or a separately defined aggregate statistic. These outputs are not interchangeable simply because they come from the same fleet. More work on strong devices also cannot replace the observations held by weak devices, so the policy must evaluate both computational contribution and population coverage.

The scale challenges extend beyond device heterogeneity to coordination overhead. Federated learning does not run a consensus protocol among millions of clients, nor does hierarchical aggregation perform local consensus. Regional aggregators reduce fan-in by validating an eligible cohort and combining updates before forwarding a partial aggregate; agreement on an ordered replicated log, if needed for the coordinator's own metadata, remains a separate control-plane service. Edge infrastructure can provide aggregation points, but each added tier creates another trust boundary and another place where weighting, clipping, privacy accounting, and failure recovery must remain consistent.

Tiering interacts with the participation bias analyzed under client scheduling (@sec-edge-intelligence-client-scheduling-f675). Capability-based selection shortens rounds but concentrates completed updates on strong devices, so stratified sampling across tiers must be paired with per-cohort evaluation of completed participation and model quality. Availability also has a daily rhythm; devices that charge overnight in one time zone form a different cohort from those available during another zone's working hours.

Orchestration brings device updates, data selection, and federated participation into one deployment policy. If that policy permits repeated adaptation, the components interact over time: earlier updates change the model, replay determines which observations persist, and participation determines which clients influence the next shared version. Continual learning must manage these accumulated effects rather than treating each update as an isolated event.

## Continual Adaptation Under Edge Budgets {#sec-edge-intelligence-bioinspired-learning-efficiency-55ad}

A keyboard model that adapts each night for a year passes through hundreds of admitted update windows, and each window moves it a little further from the version that was validated at release. Every update the chapter has built so far was judged one at a time, by whether it fit the memory budget, passed the admission test, and improved a local metric. Repeated across a deployment's lifetime, those individually acceptable updates compound. Earlier changes alter what later updates start from, the replay buffer decides which old observations still count, and participation decides which devices shape the next shared version.

The mechanisms that keep this trajectory stable are the ones already introduced, now applied over time. Selective updates bound how far any one window can move the model, and they save work only when the execution path can skip it. Replay protects earlier behavior at the cost of retained examples and additional training. Opportunistic admission delays learning until device conditions permit it. Each needs a resource budget and an outcome check on retained behavior, not only on the newest data. The long-lived stream that drives this learning is mostly unlabeled, which sets the first design question.

### Unlabeled data exploitation strategies {#sec-edge-intelligence-unlabeled-data-exploitation-strategies-cded}

Unlabeled sensor streams turn continual learning into a storage and scheduling decision. Cameras, accelerometers, location sensors, and touch interaction all produce data that can support self-supervised learning\index{Self-Supervised Learning!sensor data}, and the potential volume is large. A hypothetical camera stream running continuously at 30 frames per second produces approximately 2.6 million frames daily before retention filtering, and an accelerometer sampling at 100 Hz generates 8.6 million readings. The engineering question is which traces encode stable structure worth learning from and which should expire before they crowd out model state, replay buffers, or user-facing storage.

Learning from such traces without labels requires the supervision to come from the data's own structure. Contrastive learning\index{Contrastive Learning!definition} is the common way to manufacture it on a sensor stream, training a representation to bring designated positive pairs closer and distinguish them from designated negative pairs. Nearby camera frames or augmented views of one frame can supply positives when they preserve the task-relevant content; scene changes can invalidate that assumption. Different frames or replay entries can supply negatives, but may depict the same underlying event. The pair-selection policy therefore defines a learning signal that needs validation. Other devices' samples are not automatically available under a federated data-locality policy, and stored pairs or representations compete with replay and model state for memory.

### Continual adaptation and catastrophic forgetting {#sec-edge-intelligence-lifelong-adaptation-without-forgetting-9200}

When a deployment uses continual adaptation to address changing environments, user behavior, or task requirements, each update must balance new evidence against previously learned behavior. This is the stability-plasticity trade-off\index{Stability-plasticity trade-off!continual learning}: models must remain stable enough to preserve useful knowledge while plastic enough to learn new patterns.

Continual learning on edge devices faces several interconnected challenges. Catastrophic forgetting (@sec-edge-intelligence-experience-replay-737e) is magnified when devices cannot store or revisit historical training data. Task interference compounds it when several learning objectives compete for limited parameter capacity, and distribution shift between pretraining and local deployment demands continued adaptation without eroding the model's core representations. Restricted device memory rules out the comprehensive replay buffers that centralized infrastructure can afford.

Three families of mechanisms manage the stability-plasticity trade-off during continual learning\index{Continual learning!edge devices}. Elastic weight consolidation[^fn-ewc-continual-learning] [@kirkpatrick2017] mitigates catastrophic forgetting by penalizing changes to weights important for previous tasks, experience replay (@sec-edge-intelligence-experience-replay-737e) maintains stability during adaptation by interleaving new training with replayed examples from previous tasks, and progressive neural architectures allocate new capacity for new tasks rather than forcing all knowledge into fixed-capacity networks [@rusu2016progressive]. That last option is attractive when interference is severe, but it consumes additional memory and therefore fits only devices with enough spare capacity.

[^fn-ewc-continual-learning]: **EWC (Elastic Weight Consolidation)**\index{Elastic Weight Consolidation!definition}: Uses a diagonal approximation to the Fisher information to weight a penalty on changes from previously learned parameters [@kirkpatrick2017]. In addition to current parameters, a basic implementation stores importance scores and reference parameter values. Retaining separate penalties for earlier tasks can increase that state further. Compared with replay, EWC trades stored examples for parameter-sized statistics; which uses less memory depends on model size, retained history, precision, and the penalty implementation.

The earlier mechanisms bound each step without guaranteeing the trajectory. Meta-learned initializations (@sec-edge-intelligence-federated-personalization-3c73) and few-shot adaptation (@sec-edge-intelligence-fewshot-learning-data-streaming-566e) reach useful local behavior in few updates, and restricting updates to bias terms, adapters, or heads (@sec-edge-intelligence-model-adaptation-6a82) keeps the base parameters intact while useful pretrained representations reduce what the device must learn [@bommasani2021opportunities]. Yet even one update to a head or adapter can change predictions on earlier tasks, and a year of individually small updates can add up to a large change. The acceptance test for each window must therefore measure retained capability alongside improvement on the new data, against a recoverable baseline, because neither a small update count nor a frozen backbone is a stability guarantee.

Once the update footprint is bounded, the runtime must decide when the update can execute and whether it should be shared. The admission condition in @eq-edge-background-admission already governs when a continual update may run; what changes over a long deployment is that each admitted window also moves the device further from its last validated state. When the device also shares updates, the compression and selective transmission of @sec-edge-intelligence-bandwidthaware-update-compression-7730 keep that repeated traffic inside the bandwidth and energy budgets [@konevcny2016federated].

Stability then becomes a state-management problem. Replay buffers, support sets, adaptation logs, and model update metadata must be protected against unauthorized access or tampering because they encode the local evidence that shaped the model. Lightweight encryption or hardware-backed secure storage can reduce that exposure, but security controls do not prove that adaptation remains beneficial. Lightweight validation techniques, including confidence scoring, drift detection heuristics [@gama2014], and shadow model evaluation, monitor adaptation dynamics and can hold an update for validated review before severe degradation occurs. Robust rollback procedures require a trusted baseline checkpoint that can be restored quickly, especially in safety-important and regulated domains where failure recovery must be provable.

Privacy and compliance requirements close the loop. User consent, data minimization, retention limits, and the right to erasure must be designed into the adaptation pipeline rather than added after deployment. Meeting regulatory obligations at scale demands on-device learning workflows that preserve auditable autonomy\index{Auditable autonomy!compliance}: the model can adapt in place, but the system still retains enough control to explain, bound, and reverse that adaptation when necessary.

A design rule describes what a single device should do. A fleet applies these rules on flagship phones, budget phones, and microcontroller sensors at once, so the pillars and their stability controls must be assembled into one policy whose terms change with the device that runs it.

## Integrating the Edge Intelligence Pillars {#sec-edge-intelligence-pillar-integration-7e21}

Consider the voice assistant from the opening of this chapter, now deployed across `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.fleet_devices_million_str` that range from flagship phones to budget handsets. The chapter built model adaptation, data efficiency, and federated coordination as separate pillars, and treated separately, each solves its own constraint while leaving the others free to misbehave. An adapter rank chosen without regard to replay memory can crowd out the buffer that protects earlier behavior, and an update format chosen without regard to aggregation can produce arrays no coordinator can combine. The integration that works makes one per-tier policy decide how much a device may adapt, how much it may remember, and how it may participate in the fleet, because all three draw on the same memory, energy, and connectivity budget.

The model adaptation layer starts with candidate policies for the scenario's device tiers. Flagship phones (Tier 1) representing `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.flagship_share_pct_str` of the deployment receive LoRA adapters of rank `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.flagship_lora_rank_str`. Mid-tier devices (Tier 2), comprising `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.mid_tier_share_pct_str`, receive rank `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.mid_tier_lora_rank_str` adapters. Budget devices, the remaining `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.budget_share_pct_str`, use bias-only updates under a `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.budget_device_memory_limit_gb_str` memory limit. These assignments apply the device-tier framework of @sec-edge-intelligence-performance-vs-resource-tradeoffs-2be2. Budget phones receive the Tier 3 mechanism because the memory granted to background adaptation, not installed RAM, sets their tier. The voice assistant keeps one adaptation per user on a latency-sensitive speech path, so it uses mergeable LoRA on both capable tiers rather than the switchable residual adapters that suited the multi-context workload. These assignments specify an initial policy, not a demonstrated fit. Profiling must include the base model, activations, optimizer state, runtime, and foreground reserve, while local validation determines whether each update space captures useful voice variation.

The data efficiency layer allocates part of the same device budget to experience replay,\index{Experience Replay!device tiers} with candidate buffers of `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.budget_replay_buffer_mb_str` on budget devices and `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.flagship_replay_buffer_mb_str` on flagship models. Buffer coverage and retention tests determine whether these allocations preserve earlier behavior. The policy targets initial adaptation within `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.few_shot_interactions_range_str`, addressing the cold-start problem\index{Cold-Start Problem!definition}\index{Cold-Start Problem!personalization} of limited evidence for a new user. That target requires enough valid feedback, since a handful of ambiguous interactions supervises nothing. Later streaming updates are admitted only when both learning evidence and device resources permit them.

The federated coordination layer combines explicitly compatible shared state. Different adapter ranks and bias-only policies do not produce interchangeable arrays, so the coordinator needs separate compatible groups or a defined mapping to common parameters. Even equal-rank LoRA factors require a stated aggregation rule: averaging factors and then multiplying them generally differs from averaging the weight updates they represent. Tier-specific personal state can remain local. The scenario's `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.federated_lora_update_mb_str` adapter payload is smaller than the `{python} EdgeLoraParameterEfficiency.fp16_weight_footprint_gb_str` full-model payload, but downloads, repeated rounds, and protocol overhead still enter the communication budget. Each participating device must pass the energy, thermal, and foreground-latency admission tests. Raw audio can remain local while derived updates and participation metadata remain sensitive; secure aggregation, privacy accounting, access controls, and retention policies must cover that shared state.

These layers only work as a system when the integration policy protects against capability mismatch, component failure, resource conflicts, and untested emergent behavior. @Tbl-edge-integration-controls maps edge-learning integration controls\index{Edge learning!integration controls} for each system risk: hierarchical capability matching\index{Hierarchical capability matching!device tiers}, graceful degradation\index{Graceful degradation!edge adaptation}, explicit priority policy, and performance validation\index{Validation!performance}.

| **Integration risk** | **Control**                      | **Why it matters**                                                                                                                                   |
|:---------------------|:---------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Capability mismatch  | Hierarchical capability matching | Deploys more sophisticated techniques on capable devices while preserving basic functionality across the full device spectrum.                       |
| Component failure    | Graceful degradation             | Keeps local adaptation useful when connectivity is poor or battery constraints force the system into a minimal adaptation mode.                      |
| Resource conflict    | Explicit priority policy         | Prevents model adaptation and replay buffers from competing for the same memory, energy, or latency budget without a predefined owner.               |
| Emergent behavior    | Performance validation           | Tests combinations of device tier, network state, and adaptation policy because integrated systems fail in ways individual techniques do not expose. |

: **Edge-Learning Integration Controls**: A tiered edge-learning deployment needs explicit controls for capability matching, graceful degradation, resource conflicts, and validation across device and network combinations. {#tbl-edge-integration-controls}

@Fig-tiered-adaptation condenses the same reasoning into three questions. The first asks how much adaptation the local change needs, so a light change stays on bias-only updates whatever the device. The second asks whether the device's compute and energy envelope can afford more than adapters, and the third asks whether the updates are valuable across devices, which decides between local-only learning and federation. Although its cards carry tier-like labels (lightweight, moderate, full), they are branches of adaptation demand, not the Tier 1--3 device classes, and the device names on each card mark typical homes for a branch. In tier terms, Tier 3 devices sit in the lightweight branch, Tier 1 and Tier 2 phones in the moderate branch, and wall-powered edge servers in the full branch. The voice-assistant policy of this section therefore spans the lightweight and moderate branches, with budget phones held to the lightweight branch by a memory limit that the flowchart does not draw. The deployable choice must still satisfy the measured working-set, runtime, and energy constraints while meeting the local quality target, and federation adds the compatibility and population-validation requirements just established.

::: {#fig-tiered-adaptation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Tiered adaptation strategy**: The flowchart routes a deployment by the adaptation the local change needs, then by the device's compute and energy envelope, then by whether updates are valuable across devices. Bias-only updates, adapters or LoRA, and partial or full fine-tuning are candidates for increasingly demanding changes on increasingly capable devices, subject to measured resource and quality budgets. The federated card names one common configuration; whether differential privacy is required depends on the deployment's threat model." fig-alt="Flowchart with diamond decision nodes branching from deployment start through adaptation, compute, and data sharing decisions."}

::: {#chk-edge-intelligence-tiered-adaptation .callout-checkpoint title="Integrating the three pillars across device tiers"}

The chapter built three pillars for on-device learning: model adaptation (bias-only updates, adapters, full fine-tuning), data efficiency (few-shot, experience replay, compressed representations), and federated coordination (aggregation, client scheduling, secure aggregation). The decision framework in @fig-tiered-adaptation maps each technique to device-class capability and coordination pathway. Test integration of the three pillars across the same deployment.

- [ ] Device-tier capability matching: For a fleet with microcontroller wake-word sensors, smartphones, and wall-powered edge servers, map each device class to the branch of @fig-tiered-adaptation it can afford and state what fails when one technique is pushed across all three classes.
- [ ] Fairness in federated participation: When 90 percent of a federated round's compute comes from the top 10 percent of devices by capability, distinguish compute share from aggregation weight, identify the population-coverage risk, and select a scheduling or weighting control from the federated coordination pillar.
- [ ] Drift detection without labels: For a deployed personalization model with no ground-truth labels at the edge, describe how the device can detect enough local distribution shift to warrant a federated round using only signals available to the on-device inference path.
- [ ] Secure aggregation's participation floor: With a secure-aggregation floor of 100 devices and only 30 active devices in a given hour, determine the system response and identify which pillar must compensate.
- [ ] The auditable-autonomy trade-off: Separate the signals a central operator can observe from the device state that must remain hidden, and locate the catastrophic forgetting risk in that split.

:::

The hardest edge-learning failures appear when model adaptation, data efficiency, and federated coordination interact rather than when any one pillar fails alone. While these adaptation, efficiency, and coordination techniques solve individual constraints, they also create interaction failures in real deployments: an adapter can fit memory yet overfit sparse local data, a replay buffer can stabilize learning yet leak sensitive history, and a federated round can improve the global model while amplifying participation bias. These limits provide critical context for deciding when on-device learning is appropriate and when a simpler strategy is safer.

A tiered policy is still a design. Centralized training can standardize hardware, curate data, and validate a model before release; this policy instead ships to millions of devices whose runtimes, update histories, and connectivity differ, and it keeps changing the model after release. Shipping it turns each tier assignment into a release artifact that must be versioned, validated without central labels, and rolled back when an adapted model degrades.

## Production Integration {#sec-edge-intelligence-production-integration-beb5}

A prototype can fine-tune an adapter on one Raspberry Pi under controlled conditions. Deploying adaptation across `{python} EdgeAdaptationTierProfile.fleet_devices_million_str` requires release tests for different runtimes, resource budgets, and update histories. The production artifact must specify what each device may learn, how the result is validated, and how to restore a trusted state when adaptation fails.

### MLOps integration challenges {#sec-edge-intelligence-mlops-integration-challenges-bb4e}

Integrating on-device learning into machine learning operations (MLOps\index{MLOps!definition}), the practices that version, deploy, monitor, and roll back production models, expands what a release must validate. Backbones, adapters, update policies, and local histories can change on different schedules across heterogeneous devices. Existing integration tests, version registries, and monitoring remain useful, but the released weights no longer fully describe the behavior that will run later. Operations must validate the permitted adaptation process and its recovery path as well as the initial model.

@Fig-edge-mlops-pipeline traces a five-stage edge learning lifecycle: centralized base-model pretraining (Stage 1), per-tier hardware compression (Stage 2), and staged over-the-air rollouts (Stage 3) originate in the cloud, while local adaptation executes on-device under the released update policy (Stage 4). Aggregate telemetry (Stage 5) supplies evidence for deciding whether cloud retraining is warranted. The telemetry needs its own privacy controls; aggregation alone does not establish a privacy guarantee, and a detected change must be distinguished from a quality regression before triggering a new training cycle.

::: {#fig-edge-mlops-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Edge MLOps lifecycle pipeline**: The lifecycle links cloud pretraining and model compression with over-the-air deployment, on-device adaptation, and telemetry governed by explicit privacy controls. Keeping raw user data local does not by itself make the returned metrics private." fig-alt="Five numbered stages. In the cloud region: 1 pretrain, base model; 2 compress, per-tier packages; 3 staged rollout, over the air. An amber arrow crosses a dashed boundary into the device region: 4 adapt locally, adapter plus policy. A dashed violet loop labeled no raw data returns from the device to 5 telemetry, aggregate metrics, and continues as a retrain trigger back to stage 1."}
![](images/svg/edge-mlops-pipeline.svg)

:::

#### Deployment pipeline transformations {#sec-edge-intelligence-deployment-pipeline-transformations-431d}

A release that enables local learning includes an adaptation policy alongside model artifacts. For example, the voice-assistant policy of @sec-edge-intelligence-pillar-integration-7e21 assigns bias-only updates to budget devices and different LoRA ranks to mid-tier and flagship phones. These are conditional assignments: model footprint, runtime support, and live admission tests determine whether a device may execute them. CI/CD must therefore validate the selection logic and permitted update behavior across device configurations, not only the initial weights.

Versioning must preserve relationships among those artifacts. A local adapter belongs to a particular base model, training policy, and representation schema; a replay buffer may also depend on the encoder that produced its features. Federated round identifiers record which shared version produced a returned contribution. Updating the base therefore requires a decision to retain, migrate, retrain, or discard dependent local state. A newer version number alone does not establish compatibility, and rollback must restore a compatible set of artifacts rather than independently selecting older files.

#### Monitoring system evolution {#sec-edge-intelligence-monitoring-system-evolution-94c9}

Traditional monitoring practices aggregate metrics from centralized inference servers. On-device learning monitoring must operate within fundamentally different constraints that reshape how systems observe, measure, and respond to model behavior across distributed device populations.

Fleet telemetry for edge devices, including federated analytics\index{Federated Analytics!privacy-preserving telemetry} that report aggregate or differentially private summaries, belongs to fleet operations and is developed in @sec-ml-operations-scale-managing-edge-fleet-c591. Adaptation adds local model states that the operator may not observe centrally. Monitoring must distinguish a change in behavior from a change in quality. Unlabeled signals can identify divergence, while deciding whether the adapted model is better requires validated outcome evidence.

Drift detection\index{Drift Detection!on-device models} presents additional challenges without access to ground truth labels. While traditional monitoring compares model predictions against labeled validation sets maintained on centralized infrastructure, on-device systems must detect drift using only the indirect local signals available during deployment. Confidence calibration\index{Confidence Calibration!drift detection} compares output probabilities with eventual outcomes whenever labels exist; without verified outcomes, confidence shifts merely flag an altered score distribution. In parallel, input distribution monitoring applies statistical tests to detect when runtime feature distributions diverge from pretraining data without requiring labels. Task performance proxies use implicit feedback such as user corrections or session abandonment, though only after validating the causal link to task quality and accounting for how model suggestions alter subsequent user behavior. Finally, shadow baseline comparisons run a frozen base model alongside the adapted one; @sec-edge-intelligence-validation-strategy-adaptation-ab3d develops why that comparison measures divergence rather than quality.

Cohort evaluation must separate contribution from benefit. A device that never trains can still download an improved shared model, but its users' data may be poorly represented among the completed updates. Participation metrics reveal that coverage gap; per-cohort quality measurements establish whether it harms those users. A favorable global average cannot substitute for either measurement.

#### Continuous training orchestration {#sec-edge-intelligence-continuous-training-orchestration-8974}

Continuous training on devices combines fleet-level round or release schedules with local admission decisions. A coordinator can request work, but a device trains only when its resource and availability tests pass. The orchestrator must therefore track eligible work and compatible state without assuming simultaneous execution across clients.

The state that matters is per-device. Devices often operate on different base model versions simultaneously, creating version skew that the aggregation protocol must handle without forcing all devices to maintain identical model states. State reconciliation becomes necessary when devices reconnect after extended offline periods, potentially days or weeks. A returned update must identify its base version so the coordinator can reject it, apply a stated staleness policy, or request new training from the current base. Accumulated personal adaptations, including per-device adapters and replay buffers, carry their own version tags and need not be merged into the shared model.

Resource-aware scheduling applies @eq-edge-background-admission at fleet scale. Federated rounds usually add idle, charging, and unmetered-network requirements on top of the local admission test, and a daily energy cap bounds cumulative learning cost across many admitted windows.

Admission also has a runtime half. Bias updates in early layers require backward computation through later operations; head-only adaptation confines that computation to the head. Either path competes with inference for compute, memory bandwidth, and thermal headroom on a shared SoC. Users judge the device by its quality of service (QoS),\index{Quality of Service!definition} so the runtime gives inference priority and throttles or revokes a training window as foreground latency approaches its deadline. At the microcontroller extreme, measured update energy and available reserves determine how much learning a duty-cycled or harvested-power budget can support.[^fn-mcu-milliwatt-power]

[^fn-mcu-milliwatt-power]: **Microcontroller Power Budget**\index{Microcontroller Power Budget!definition}\index{Microcontroller!power budget and duty cycling}: In an illustrative operating point, 10 mW of active training for 10 seconds consumes 0.1 J. The number of updates that fit that session requires a measured time or energy per update. Battery lifetime additionally depends on usable capacity under the actual load, sleep power, radio activity, conversion losses, and duty cycle; nameplate capacity alone does not establish continuous-training lifetime.

When a representative central validation set is unavailable, federated evaluation can aggregate metrics computed on local held-out data. Update magnitudes provide an optimization diagnostic, but small changes can reflect stalled learning rather than acceptable quality. Participation audits must accompany outcome measurements so that apparent progress is not confined to an overrepresented cohort.

#### Validation strategy adaptation {#sec-edge-intelligence-validation-strategy-adaptation-ab3d}

Traditional validation approaches assume access to held-out test sets and centralized evaluation infrastructure where model quality can be measured directly against known ground truth. On-device learning requires distributed validation that respects privacy and resource constraints while still providing reliable quality signals across heterogeneous device populations.

Shadow model\index{Shadow Model!evaluation} evaluation maintains multiple model variants on each device and compares their behavior. Devices can run a frozen, last-known-good model beside a locally adapted version and measure prediction divergence, confidence shifts, latency, and resource use on the same input stream. Without labels or a validated outcome proxy, these comparisons detect change, not performance degradation: agreement can hide a shared error, and disagreement does not reveal which model is correct. A shadow comparison can therefore suspend an update for further evaluation, but automatic rollback requires labeled outcomes, a validated behavioral invariant, or a proxy whose relationship to task quality has been established for the deployment.

The comparator can therefore act only as a gate, never as a judge (@fig-shadow-validation). The live input stream is mirrored to the frozen baseline and the adapted candidate, and the comparator tracks their disagreement, confidence shift, and resource deltas. When disagreement exceeds a tolerance $\tau$, the gate holds the candidate out of service; validated outcome evidence then either clears it or confirms the regression that justifies rollback.

::: {#fig-shadow-validation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**On-device shadow validation**: A frozen baseline runs beside the active model. Their disagreement, confidence, latency, and resource deltas can flag a change without labels; a rollback decision still requires a validated outcome signal or safety invariant." fig-alt="Flow diagram with a data stream forking to frozen baseline and active models, both feeding a comparator whose change signal can hold an update for validated review."}
